author: Alkarim Billawala / alkarim.billawala.ca
weeks: Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders

questions.stem: A second-year medical student is preparing a wellness talk and wants to quote the course's Statistics Canada figures. She has one slide for lifetime prevalence of mood or anxiety disorders among Canadians. Which figure belongs on it?
questions.explain: Why: the pre-week reading quotes Statistics Canada twice — 1 in 3 Canadians will meet criteria for any mental health or substance use disorder, and within that 1 in 5 (21.3%) for a mood or anxiety disorder. Not the others: one in three is the broader any-disorder figure; one in eight is the WHO worldwide figure quoted in Week 40 for any mental disorder; one in ten is not a figure the course gives.

questions.stem: A third-year resident describes feeling emotionally drained after every call shift, increasingly detached and cynical toward patients, and convinced that nothing she does at work makes a difference. Which combination defines the syndrome she is describing?
options: Emotional exhaustion, depersonalization and a low sense of personal accomplishment
questions.explain: Why: the module defines burnout as a syndrome of three dimensions after Maslach — emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a low sense of personal accomplishment — developing in response to enduring work-related stress. Not the others: low mood, anhedonia and insomnia are depressive symptoms; absenteeism and errors are consequences of burnout, not its definition; fatigue and poor concentration are non-specific.

questions.stem: Two residents are assessed in the same week. The first feels cynical, exhausted and ineffective on the wards but reports feeling like herself again within days of starting a two-week vacation. The second has felt low and joyless for six weeks, including throughout a recent holiday, and has stopped seeing friends. According to the module's discriminator, how should the two be classified?
options: The first has burnout; the second has depression
The first has depression; the second has burnout
questions.explain: Why: the module's single discriminator is context: burnout's negative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are associated with work and improve away from it; depression's are pervasive and persistent across settings. Symptoms that lift on holiday point to burnout; symptoms that persist through a holiday point to depression. Not the others: the two presentations differ exactly on the feature the module uses to separate them.

questions.stem: A hospital wellness committee is told that medical students must simply be a more vulnerable group than their peers, which is why their rates of depression are higher. Which finding from the module most directly contradicts this explanation?
options: 27% of medical students report depression or depressive symptoms
Students accepted to medical school have lower rates of depression and burnout than similar-aged peers before training starts
Only 15.7% of depressed medical students seek treatment
questions.explain: Why: the module presents the pre-training data specifically to foreclose a selection effect: matriculants start with lower rates of depression and burnout than age-matched peers, and stress during medical school then raises the risk. The excess distress is therefore attributable to training, not to who enters medicine. Not the others: the 27%, 15.7% and 38% figures describe prevalence and help-seeking during or after training; none speaks to baseline vulnerability.

guide.s: lower rates of depression and burnout

questions.stem: A question asks for the proportion of Canadian residents who screened positive for depression in the 2018 CMA National Physician Health Survey. Which figure does the module give?
questions.explain: Why: the CMA survey figures are 38% burnout, 48% positive depression screen, and 15% suicidal ideation in the past year. Not the others: 27% is the medical-student depression prevalence from Rotenstein 2016; 38% is the Canadian residents' burnout figure; 15% is their past-year suicidal ideation.

questions.stem: A clerk who screened positive for depression on a wellness survey explains why he has not sought care: he worries the diagnosis could reach his program director, affect his residency match, and lead to mandatory monitoring by the licensing body. According to the module, what single construct underlies the barriers he describes?
questions.explain: Why: the module lists six barriers — lack of time, cost, confidentiality concerns, potential career implications, exposure to unwanted interventions, and more unwanted licensing or supervision oversight — and draws them all down into one word, stigma. The clerk names three of the four professional-consequence barriers. Not the others: lack of time and cost are practical barriers on the same list but are not what he describes, and access to psychiatrists is not one of the module's six.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old nurse has avoided elevators for years, taking the stairs even to the fourteenth floor, and once endured a single elevator ride 'shaking and certain it would drop'. She has now declined a supervisory position because the new unit is only reachable by elevator. Which DSM-5 criterion does the declined position most directly satisfy?
options: A: marked fear about a specific object or situation
C: the situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear
E: the fear has lasted six months or more
F: clinically significant distress or impairment in occupational function
questions.explain: Why: turning down the position is occupational impairment, criterion F — the element that converts a tolerable dislike into a disorder, exactly as Stuart's declined promotion does in the module's case. Not the others: the fear of elevators is A, the stair-climbing and the endured ride are C, and the years of history are E; each is met, but the question asks which criterion the declined position satisfies.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old refuses to attend birthday parties because a costumed mascot might be present, screaming and hiding when one appears at a shopping centre. Which specifier applies?
questions.explain: Why: the module's five specifiers are animal, natural environment, blood-injection-injury, situational and other, and costumed characters are the module's own example under other, alongside choking, vomiting and loud noises. Not the others: situational covers airplanes, elevators and enclosed spaces; animal covers insects, spiders and dogs; natural environment covers heights, storms and water.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with a phobia of needles that has led him to skip vaccinations and blood tests asks what treatment has the best evidence. Which is the module's answer?
options: A short course of lorazepam before each procedure
An SSRI titrated over several months
Cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure
questions.explain: Why: the module states that CBT is the gold-standard treatment for specific phobia, delivered as systematic desensitization up a fear hierarchy, and that there is little evidence to support medication in most cases. Not the others: no drug is named anywhere in the module; benzodiazepines, SSRIs and beta blockers all belong to other disorders' treatment slides this week.

questions.stem: A patient with a spider phobia has just become comfortable looking at a live spider in a jar, which she had rated 5 out of 10. According to the module's example hierarchy, which exposure comes next?
options: Touch the jar containing the spider
Stand two feet from a live spider
questions.explain: Why: the hierarchy runs picture 1/10 → rubber spider 3/10 → live spider in a jar 5/10 → touch the jar 8/10 → stand two feet away 9/10 → touch a live spider 10/10, and exposure moves up one level once the current level is tolerated. Not the others: the rubber spider is below her current level; standing two feet away and touching the spider are two and three steps further up.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman avoids crowded malls, buses and cinemas because she fears she could not get out or get help if she became unwell, and now leaves home only with her husband. She has no fear of any single object. Which diagnosis on the specific phobia differential best fits?
questions.explain: Why: fear of being unable to escape or get help across multiple situation types, with dependence on a companion, is agoraphobia, the first item on the module's differential. Not the others: a situational specific phobia is fear of one circumscribed situation, not a cluster of them; social anxiety disorder is fear of negative evaluation; panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks not tied to a cue, and none are described.

guide.s: unable to escape or get help

questions.stem: A 19-year-old university student has stopped attending tutorials and eating in the cafeteria. She describes intense worry that others will notice her hands trembling or her face flushing and think she is 'pathetic'. She has no fear of the classroom itself and no unexpected attacks. Which feature makes social anxiety disorder the best diagnosis rather than specific phobia or agoraphobia?
options: The avoidance has lasted more than six months
The fear is of being negatively evaluated, including for the visible anxiety itself
The symptoms are out of proportion to the actual threat
She has stopped eating in public
questions.explain: Why: criterion B — fear of acting in a way, or showing anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated — is the core of social anxiety disorder and the discriminator from specific phobia (fear of the object or situation itself) and agoraphobia (fear of being unable to escape or get help). Not the others: duration and disproportion are shared by all three anxiety disorders; avoiding eating in public is an example of avoidance, not the discriminating fear.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old sales manager has severe anxiety only when giving quarterly presentations to the board; he socializes comfortably, dines out, and has no other feared situations. He asks for a first-line medication. Which is the module's answer?
options: Propranolol taken as needed before presentations
questions.explain: Why: fear restricted to speaking or performing in public is the performance-only specifier, and the module's flowchart routes it to propranolol PRN, taken before the performance. Not the others: the daily SSRIs, venlafaxine XR and pregabalin are the first-line options on the generalized branch, for patients whose fear extends across social situations.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman reports racing heart, breathlessness and chest tightness that arrive without warning, including while asleep and while alone at home; between attacks she worries constantly about the next one. She is comfortable in social settings. Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?
options: Social anxiety disorder with panic attacks
questions.explain: Why: recurrent unexpected panic attacks — occurring during sleep and when alone, with no social cue — plus worry about further attacks is panic disorder. Not the others: social anxiety with panic attacks requires the attacks to be cued by social situations, as Lindsay's are before presentations; a situational phobia needs one circumscribed situation; GAD is worry about multiple everyday matters, not discrete attacks.

questions.stem: A parent asks at what age social anxiety disorder most often begins. Which figure does the module give as the median age of onset?
questions.explain: Why: the module gives a median age of onset of 13, with 75% beginning between 7 and 15. Not the others: 7 is the lower bound of that range; 30 is the median onset of GAD, the contrast the week's quizzes draw; 18 is not a figure in the module.

questions.stem: A resident is asked which SSRI appears on the first-line list for generalized social anxiety disorder but not on the GAD first-line list in this week's modules. Which is it?
questions.explain: Why: the social anxiety flowchart names escitalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine and paroxetine; the GAD list names escitalopram, paroxetine and sertraline. Fluvoxamine is the one that appears only in the social anxiety list. Not the others: escitalopram and sertraline are first line in both modules; fluoxetine appears in neither list and features only as Lindsay's past antidepressant.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with Parkinson's disease avoids restaurants because his tremor makes eating in front of others difficult, and he is embarrassed when it is noticed. His avoidance is limited to meals out and is proportionate to the visibility of his tremor. According to criterion J, how should this be classified?
options: Not social anxiety disorder, because the fear is related and proportionate to a visible medical condition
questions.explain: Why: criterion J states that when another medical condition such as Parkinson's disease, obesity or disfigurement is present, the fear must be clearly unrelated or excessive to count. Fear that is related and proportionate to a visible tremor does not meet the criterion. Not the others: neither specifier applies when the diagnosis itself is not met, and there is no phobic object.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old teacher has worried most days for eight months about her finances, her students' outcomes and her health, and says she cannot switch the worry off. She reports restlessness and muscle tension but sleeps well, concentrates adequately, is not irritable and is not unusually tired. Does she meet the module's criteria for GAD?
options: Yes: worry for more than six months is sufficient on its own
Yes: two of the six associated symptoms with uncontrollable worry meets the threshold
No: at least three of the six associated symptoms are required
No: the worry must be about a single domain
questions.explain: Why: the module's third criterion requires three or more of six associated symptoms (restlessness, easy fatigue, concentration or mind going blank, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance). She has two — restlessness and muscle tension — so the count is not met despite eight months of uncontrollable worry. Not the others: duration and uncontrollability are necessary but not sufficient; GAD is worry about a number of events, so multiple domains fit rather than exclude.

questions.stem: Which statement about the epidemiology of GAD matches the module?
options: Lifetime prevalence is about 3%, and it usually begins in childhood
Lifetime prevalence is about 9%, with a median age of onset of 30 and a 2:1 female predominance
Lifetime prevalence is about 20%, with equal sex distribution
It is the most common anxiety disorder and begins at a median age of 13
questions.explain: Why: the module's quizzes and epidemiology slide give 9% lifetime prevalence, median onset 30 (later than the other anxiety disorders, very unlikely before adolescence), and females twice as likely, 2:1. Not the others: 3% and 20% are distractors from the module's own prevalence quiz; median onset 13 is social anxiety disorder; specific phobia, not GAD, is the most common anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with six months of anxiety, palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor and a 5 kg weight loss despite a good appetite. Before diagnosing GAD, which item on the module's differential should be addressed first?
options: Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition, such as hyperthyroidism
questions.explain: Why: the module's differential leads with anxiety disorder due to another medical condition and names hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma; heat intolerance, tremor and weight loss with a preserved appetite are the classic thyroid picture. Not the others: substance-induced anxiety is second on the list but nothing in the stem suggests caffeine or medication; social anxiety and OCD have no supporting features here.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed GAD prefers to start with psychotherapy. Which pair does the module recommend most?
options: Cognitive behavioural therapy and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
questions.explain: Why: the module's multi-select quiz keys CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy as the two therapies to recommend most. Not the others: exposure, relaxation, biofeedback, imagery and psychoeducation are all on the module's treatment list but are not the top two; psychodynamic psychotherapy is the one option that appears nowhere on the list.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with GAD, atrial fibrillation on a beta blocker, a documented rash to paroxetine and a good past response to sertraline for depression is to start medication. According to the module's first-line list and his history, which agent is the most appropriate choice?
questions.explain: Why: the module's first-line agents are the SSRIs escitalopram, paroxetine and sertraline, the SNRIs venlafaxine and duloxetine, and pregabalin; the paroxetine rash removes that option, and a prior response to sertraline makes it the natural choice. Not the others: paroxetine is contraindicated by the allergy; a benzodiazepine and an antipsychotic are the module's own distractors for the drug class with the most evidence, which is an antidepressant.

questions.stem: A patient with GAD drinks four 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee daily and asks whether that is excessive. Using the module's infographic values, roughly how does his daily caffeine intake compare with the moderate range?
options: About 240 mg, within the moderate range
About 400 mg, just above the moderate range
About 540 mg, roughly double the moderate ceiling
About 800 mg, roughly triple the moderate ceiling
questions.explain: Why: the infographic gives 135 mg per 8-ounce brewed coffee and a moderate range of 200–300 mg per day; four cups is about 540 mg, roughly double the ceiling, which is why the module advises reducing caffeinated and high-sugar drinks. Not the others: 240 mg would be under two cups; 400 mg and 800 mg do not follow from the module's values.

questions.stem: Which single feature distinguishes GAD from both specific phobia and social anxiety disorder as this week's modules present them?
options: A required count of three of six associated symptoms
The need to rule out medical conditions and substances
The use of an SSRI as first-line treatment
questions.explain: Why: GAD is the only one of the three with a symptom count — three of six; specific phobia (A–G) and social anxiety disorder (A–J) require every criterion. Not the others: the six-month duration is shared by all three; ruling out organic and substance causes appears in all three differentials; SSRIs are first line in both GAD and social anxiety disorder, and no drug is supported in specific phobia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old accountant describes intrusive images of his apartment burning down. He re-checks the stove and every outlet in a fixed sequence before leaving, which takes about 20 minutes each morning; he finds the images senseless and is embarrassed by the checking. He is never late and describes only mild frustration. Which element of the OCD criteria is not clearly met?
options: B: severity, since the rituals occupy under an hour a day and cause only mild distress without impairment
Insight specifier, since he recognizes the thoughts as senseless
questions.explain: Why: criterion B requires marked distress, more than one hour a day, or significant interference with functioning; twenty minutes with mild frustration and no impairment meets none of the three limbs. Not the others: the intrusive fire images are obsessions and the sequenced checking is a compulsion performed to prevent a feared event, so criterion A is met; recognizing the thoughts as senseless describes good insight, a specifier rather than a failed criterion.

guide.s: occupy more than one hour a day

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman's home is filled to the ceilings with newspapers she cannot discard 'because one might contain a warning I will need to keep my family safe'. She also counts light switches in sets of four until the set feels complete. Which diagnosis does the module direct?
questions.explain: Why: the module's override rule: when hoarding is driven by typical OCD obsessions such as harm prevention or incompleteness — keeping papers that might prevent harm, completing a set — OCD is diagnosed instead of hoarding disorder. Not the others: hoarding disorder is exclusively about difficulty discarding and accumulation without such obsessions; OCPD has no intrusions or rituals; there is no evidence of a fixed delusion without obsessional structure.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man spends hours nightly at online poker, enjoys the excitement, and says he would only stop because of his mounting debts. His wife describes the behaviour as 'compulsive'. According to the module, what distinguishes this from an OCD compulsion?
options: It occupies more than an hour a day
He derives pleasure from the activity and resists it only because of its consequences
It is performed in response to an obsession
It is a stereotyped movement rather than a behaviour
questions.explain: Why: the module separates gambling, paraphilias and substance use from OCD compulsions on one feature: the person derives pleasure from the activity and wishes to resist it only because of its deleterious consequences; OCD compulsions are performed to reduce discomfort, not for pleasure. Not the others: the time spent does not decide the category; there is no obsession driving the poker; a stereotyped movement is a repetitive non-functional motor behaviour such as rocking.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with OCD is started on sertraline. At week 8 she reports no benefit and asks whether the drug has failed. According to the module's principles, what is the most appropriate response?
options: Stop sertraline and switch to clomipramine as first line
Continue and increase the dose: response often takes 6–12 weeks and an adequate trial is 12–15 weeks
Stop the medication abruptly and begin CBT instead
questions.explain: Why: the module's principles are to start low and aim high, to be patient because response often takes 6–12 weeks, and that an adequate trial requires 12–15 weeks; eight weeks at an unoptimized dose is not a failed trial. Not the others: clomipramine is a second-line agent, not first line; the module has no augmentation pathway; medication is discontinued very slowly, never abruptly, and CBT can be added rather than substituted.

questions.stem: A patient with OCD asks whether taking an SSRI together with CBT would work better than either alone. Which statement reflects the module's algorithm notes?
options: The combination is superior to both CBT alone and medication alone
The combination is superior to medication alone but not to CBT alone
Medication alone is superior to CBT alone
CBT adds nothing once an SSRI is started
questions.explain: Why: the algorithm's notes state that CBT is equivalent or superior to pharmacotherapy and that the combination of CBT and medication is superior to medication alone, but not to CBT alone. Not the others: each reverses one half of that statement; the module also lists higher relapse rates with medication unless behavioural strategies are combined.

questions.stem: A therapist builds a contamination hierarchy with a patient whose items run from sorting dirty laundry (25/100) to touching a public toilet seat (80/100). Which statement about the exposure process matches the module?
options: Exposure begins with the most distressing item so that habituation generalizes downward
Exposure proceeds systematically from the least distressing item upward while rituals and avoidance are prevented
Exposure is paired with performing the ritual afterward to limit distress
The hierarchy must begin at 100 to be valid
questions.explain: Why: ERP defines the triggers, ranks discomfort, builds a hierarchy with the most distressing item at the top, and then exposes the patient systematically while preventing both rituals and avoidance; treatment starts at the bottom of the hierarchy. Not the others: starting at the top is flooding, not the module's method; performing the ritual afterward is the compulsion cycle that maintains the disorder; the example hierarchy tops out at 80, so a ceiling of 100 is not required.

questions.stem: Two anxiety-over-time graphs are shown: in one, each anxiety peak is followed by a near-vertical drop to baseline and every peak is the same height; in the other, each successive peak is lower and shorter. Which pairing of graph to process is correct?
options: First graph: habituation with exposure; second graph: the compulsion cycle
First graph: the compulsion cycle; second graph: habituation with repeated exposure and response prevention
Both graphs show the compulsion cycle at different stages
Both graphs show habituation, with and without medication
questions.explain: Why: performing a compulsion produces an abrupt drop to baseline and peaks that stay the same height, the highly reinforcing cycle that maintains OCD; repeated exposure with response prevention produces peaks that are progressively lower and shorter as the patient learns the feared outcome does not occur and anxiety subsides on its own — habituation. Not the others: the shapes are the defining difference between the two processes, so they cannot both be one process.

questions.stem: Six weeks after a serious highway collision, a 44-year-old bus driver has nightly nightmares of the crash, refuses to drive on highways, feels persistently numb and detached from his family, and is irritable with poor sleep. He has stopped working. Which statement about his diagnosis is correct?
options: Acute stress disorder, because symptoms began within a month of the event
PTSD: he meets the intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and arousal thresholds and the disturbance has lasted over one month
Adjustment disorder, because the stressor was an accident rather than violence
GAD, because irritability and sleep disturbance dominate
questions.explain: Why: the criteria require at least one intrusion (nightmares), one avoidance (highways), two negative cognition or mood symptoms (persistent negative state, detachment), two arousal symptoms (irritability, sleep), a duration over one month, and impairment; six weeks past a collision with serious injury threatened satisfies all of it. Not the others: acute stress disorder is confined to the first 30 days; a collision threatening death or serious injury is a criterion-A trauma; GAD is generalized worry, not trauma-cued intrusions.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old paramedic with no single defining incident develops intrusive images, avoidance of certain call types and hypervigilance after years of attending fatal collisions. Does her exposure satisfy the trauma criterion as the module states it?
options: No, because she was never personally in danger
No, because criterion A requires witnessing the death of a family member
Yes, because repeated exposure through occupation is one of the four routes
Yes, but only if she also learned that a loved one was harmed
questions.explain: Why: the module gives four routes to exposure — direct, witnessing, learning that a traumatic event happened to a loved one, and repeated exposure through occupation — so indirect and cumulative occupational exposure qualifies. Not the others: personal danger is only one route; witnessing a family member's death is not required; the loved-one route is an alternative, not an additional condition.

questions.stem: Ten days after witnessing a fatal stabbing, a 25-year-old has flashbacks, avoids the street where it happened and startles easily. According to the module, what is the correct diagnosis at this point and the expected course?
options: PTSD; most patients remain symptomatic for years
Acute stress disorder; most patients recover, and a subset who remain symptomatic past 30 days are diagnosed with PTSD
Adjustment disorder; symptoms resolve within three months
No diagnosis; symptoms within a month of trauma are normal
questions.explain: Why: the module defines acute stress disorder as PTSD-type symptoms with functional impairment in the first 30 days after a highly traumatic event, notes that most patients recover, and that a subset with symptoms beyond 30 days are diagnosed with PTSD; time of onset is the module's distinguishing axis. Not the others: PTSD requires more than one month; adjustment disorder is not defined by the module for this; symptomatic impairment within a month is a disorder, not normal.

questions.stem: Which set of figures matches the module's PTSD epidemiology?
options: Lifetime prevalence 2–3%, mean onset 19.5, more common in males
Lifetime prevalence 6–9%, onset in the mid-to-late twenties, twice as common in females
Lifetime prevalence 9%, onset in adolescence, equal sex distribution
Lifetime prevalence 20%, onset after 40, more common in males
questions.explain: Why: the module quizzes key 6–9% lifetime prevalence (the epidemiology slide says 9%), onset typically in the mid-to-late twenties (quiz band 25–30), and twice as common in females. Not the others: 2–3% and 19.5 are OCD's numbers; the remaining sets invent figures the module does not give.

questions.stem: A patient with PTSD asks for the single most effective psychotherapy. A second patient is offered a choice limited to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, EMDR, psychodynamic psychotherapy, interpersonal therapy and relaxation therapy. According to the module's two quiz keys, what are the answers?
options: Most effective: EMDR; from the limited list: trauma-focused CBT
Most effective: trauma-focused CBT; from the limited list: EMDR
Most effective: DBT; from the limited list: relaxation therapy
Most effective: cognitive processing therapy; from the limited list: interpersonal therapy
questions.explain: Why: the module keys trauma-focused CBT as the most effective modality and names it the mainstay, and keys EMDR for Annie when trauma-focused CBT is not among the options, EMDR being the only trauma-processing therapy on that list. Not the others: DBT is listed only as a therapy aimed at self-harm in BPD; cognitive processing therapy is a valid modality but not the keyed most effective.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with PTSD is to start medication. Which option is first line in the module, and which is keyed wrong on its treatment-choice quiz?
options: First line: venlafaxine XR; wrong: a benzodiazepine
questions.explain: Why: the module's first-line agents are the SSRIs fluoxetine, paroxetine and sertraline and the SNRI venlafaxine XR, and its quiz keys antidepressant over benzodiazepine, ECT and antipsychotic. Not the others: each pairs a keyed-wrong class as first line with a first-line agent as wrong.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man develops nightmares, avoidance and hypervigilance after being beaten unconscious during a robbery; he also reports headaches, slowed thinking and memory lapses. Which item on the module's medical differential must be considered alongside PTSD?
questions.explain: Why: the module's medical differential is traumatic brain injury, if physical trauma occurred, and neurological damage; being beaten unconscious with headaches, slowed thinking and memory lapses is exactly that scenario, and the two can coexist. Not the others: hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma are the GAD module's organic mimics of anxiety; conversion disorder is on the psychiatric list, not the medical one.

questions.stem: A public-health student states that suicide rates in Canada are highest among 15-to-24-year-olds because suicide is the second leading cause of death in that group. According to the module, what is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Suicide is not a leading cause of death in that age group
The highest suicide rates are in people aged 40–59; the second-place ranking at 15–24 reflects how few other causes of death there are at that age
Suicide rates are highest over age 65
The ranking applies to attempts, not deaths
questions.explain: Why: the module states two separate facts: suicide is the second leading cause of death at ages 15–24, and the highest rates are at ages 40–59. A high ranking in the young is a ranking effect, not the highest rate. Not the others: the second-place ranking is the module's own statement; no over-65 figure is given; the ranking is about deaths.

questions.stem: Which statement about sex differences in suicide matches the module?
options: Males attempt more often and die more often
Females attempt three to four times more often, but males are more likely to die by suicide
Females attempt and die more often
questions.explain: Why: the module states that females are 3–4 times more likely to attempt suicide, while males are more likely to die by it. Not the others: each reverses or erases one half of that paradox. The module gives no mechanism for it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old divorced man with chronic back pain and heavy alcohol use is admitted after a serious overdose, his second attempt. Which of his features does the module identify as one of the most powerful predictors of suicide across all age groups?
questions.explain: Why: the module's highlighted note reads that a history of previous attempts is one of the most powerful predictors of suicide for all age groups, with the instruction always to ask about prior attempts. Not the others: pain, substance use and lack of a spouse are all SAD PERSONS risk factors present here, but the module singles out previous attempts as the strongest.

questions.stem: A clerk hesitates to ask a depressed patient about suicidal thoughts, worried that raising the topic could plant the idea. According to the module, what should the clerk do?
options: Avoid the topic unless the patient raises it first
Ask indirectly, for example 'you're not thinking of doing anything silly?'
Ask directly and calmly, using a normalizing statement first, because asking does not increase risk
Ask only if a family member is present
questions.explain: Why: the module's quiz keys as false the claim that asking increases risk, and its feedback states that bringing up the topic does not increase risk and that the clinician's own discomfort must not get in the way. Patients do not necessarily volunteer these thoughts, so the module scripts a frank, calm, normalizing approach ending in a direct question. Not the others: avoidance and oblique phrasing are the errors the module warns against.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman says she has thought about 'taking all my pills'. Which sequence of questions follows the module's first assessment step?
options: Ask about her childhood, then her family history, then her supports
Clarify whether the thoughts are passive or active, ask which pills and whether she has access to them, then ask whether she thinks she might actually do it
Ask about hope and reasons for living before anything else
Screen for depression with a symptom checklist
questions.explain: Why: step one, assess current plan and intent, separates ideation (passive versus active), then the plan and its feasibility with available means ("Which pills would you take?" "Do you have access to these pills?"), then intent and whether she has started to act. Not the others: protective factors are step four, asked after rapport; developmental history and depression screening are not part of the four-step sequence.

questions.stem: After assessing plan, intent, intensity and risk factors, a resident asks a suicidal patient, 'What has stopped you from acting on these thoughts?' Which step of the module's approach is this, and which listed protective factor can the interview itself create?
options: Step 2, intensity; access to lethal means
Step 4, protective factors; a strong therapeutic alliance
questions.explain: Why: the question is one of the module's three scripted step four questions for eliciting hope and ambivalence, and the protective factors listed are children, spouse or family, pets, religious beliefs, intact self-esteem, and a strong therapeutic alliance, the one factor the clinician creates in the encounter. Not the others: access to lethal means is a risk factor; the other pairings mis-assign the step.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man develops persistent low mood, loss of interest and poor energy beginning three days after a left middle cerebral artery stroke, before he has learned the extent of his deficits. Which diagnosis does the module's reasoning support?
options: Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
questions.explain: Why: the module's quiz keys post-stroke mood change with onset days after the event as a direct pathophysiological consequence, describing post-stroke depression as independent of the psychological effects of acquired disability; the time course tracks the event. Not the others: an adjustment reaction would follow awareness of the disability; a primary depressive disorder is excluded by criterion C when the medical cause is evident; there is no fluctuating inattention to suggest delirium.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman becomes tearful, hopeless and withdrawn beginning three weeks after being told she has a thyroid cancer that imaging suggests has been present for over a year. Which statement reflects the module's reasoning?
options: This is a depressive disorder due to another medical condition because the symptoms began after a medical diagnosis
This is most likely a psychological reaction to the diagnosis, because the tumour predated the mood change and the symptoms track the news rather than the pathophysiology
This is a medication-induced depressive disorder
questions.explain: Why: the module's testicular-cancer item makes exactly this point: the cancer was present for some time before the diagnosis, so mood symptoms beginning after the diagnosis most likely represent a psychological reaction to being diagnosed, not a direct pathophysiological consequence. Not the others: timing from the diagnosis is the trap; there is no inattention or medication to implicate.

questions.stem: Which statement about the DSM-5 criteria for disorders due to another medical condition is correct?
options: Each disorder has its own version of all five criteria
Only criterion A differs between the depressive, bipolar and anxiety forms; criteria B to E are the same
A two-week duration and five of nine symptoms are required for the depressive form
Symptoms occurring only during delirium still qualify
questions.explain: Why: the module states that the symptoms under criterion A depend on the specific disorder while criteria B–E remain the same: pathophysiological evidence, not better explained by another disorder, not exclusively during delirium, and distress, impairment, hospitalization or psychotic features. Not the others: the disorder-specific criterion A variants carry no symptom counts or durations; symptoms confined to delirium are excluded by criterion D.

guide.s: Criterion A is the only disorder-specific criterion

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV develops persistent depressed mood two weeks after starting a new antiretroviral regimen; his viral load is well controlled and he has no history of drug use. Following the module's HIV example, which label fits best?
options: Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
questions.explain: Why: the module's HIV figure assigns three biological pathways three different labels: virus on the CNS → due to another medical condition; antiretroviral effect on the CNS → medication-induced; comorbid drug use → substance-induced. Onset after a new antiretroviral with controlled disease and no drug use points to the medication. Not the others: each names a different pathway than the one described.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with no psychiatric history develops new, recurrent, untriggered panic attacks. Which of the module's three diagnostic factors does her presentation most directly raise?
options: Atypical features: onset outside the typical risk period
questions.explain: Why: the module lists time course, atypical features and a plausible pathophysiological mechanism, and its own example of an atypical feature is onset of panic disorder symptoms at age 70, outside the typical risk period and therefore a red flag for a medical cause. Not the others: nothing in the stem yet describes a medical condition's course or mechanism.

questions.stem: Which condition appears in the module's lists of causes of both depressive and manic symptoms?
questions.explain: Why: four conditions appear in both the depressive and manic columns: stroke, traumatic brain injury, Cushing's disease and HIV infection. Not the others: Parkinson's disease is listed only under depressive symptoms; multiple sclerosis only under manic; hyperthyroidism only under anxiety.

questions.stem: A student argues that Nazi physicians must have abandoned their medical ethics entirely in order to take part in genocide. According to the module, what is wrong with this view?
options: Most Nazi physicians were coerced and acted against their beliefs
They reinterpreted their duty to preserve life through dehumanization, seeing genocide as a 'therapeutic imperative' for society
Only a small minority of German doctors joined the Nazi party
Their ethics were suspended by law during wartime
questions.explain: Why: the module's thesis is that Nazi doctors did not think genocide contravened their commitment to life; their racism and dehumanization let them see it as helping society, a "therapeutic imperative", exemplified by Fritz Klein's gangrenous-appendix metaphor. Not the others: the German Medical Association documented support without coercion, and more than half of German doctors were early party members; wartime law is not the module's explanation.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the origin of modern research ethics as the module presents it?
options: Tuskegee study → Nuremberg Code → Declaration of Helsinki
Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg (1946) → Nuremberg Code → Declaration of Helsinki
Declaration of Helsinki → Nuremberg Code → Belmont Report
Belmont Report → Nuremberg Code → Doctors' Trial
questions.explain: Why: the Doctors' Trial of 1946, in which 20 of 23 defendants were physicians, led to the Nuremberg Code, the first generally accepted code for research on human subjects (ten conditions including informed consent), which heavily informed the Declaration of Helsinki. Not the others: Tuskegee is the American chain that produced the Belmont Report of 1979, a separate lineage.

questions.stem: On a ward round a resident refers to a patient as 'the cirrhotic in bed 4' and remarks that 'he did this to himself'. Which lesson from the module does this illustrate?
options: Dehumanizing discourse: discussing patients as their problems and blaming them for their conditions
questions.explain: Why: the module's list of dehumanizing discourse in medicine includes discussing patients as their problems ("the heart failure in room 32") and blaming patients for their conditions, such as people who drink or use drugs, so that they receive less sympathy. Not the others: the remark is neither about inherited trauma, nor about resisting authority, nor about research.

questions.stem: Which detail of the Tuskegee syphilis study most directly shows that the harm continued after a cure was available?
options: The men were told they had 'bad blood'
Penicillin became the standard treatment by 1947 but was withheld until the study ended in 1972
The men were recruited through a free healthcare initiative
questions.explain: Why: the module states that penicillin had become the standard treatment for syphilis by 1947, yet the team withheld it, withheld information, and blocked access to treatment elsewhere until a whistleblower ended the study in 1972. Not the others: the deception, the start date and the recruitment method describe the design, not the continuation past a cure.

questions.stem: A question asks for the figure the module gives on the disproportionate sterilization of Indigenous and Métis people in Alberta between 1969 and 1972. Which is it?
options: More than 25% of those sterilized while only 2.5% of the population
questions.explain: Why: the module states that from 1969 to 1972 Indigenous and Métis people accounted for more than 25% of sterilized patients but only 2.5% of the population, a ten-fold overrepresentation, under Alberta's Sexual Sterilization Act (1928–1972), which sterilized over 2,800 women in total. Not the others: 2,800 is the total across all women, not all Indigenous; 70% is the tuberculosis mortality figure from residential schools.

questions.stem: A clerk is told to perform an educational pelvic examination on an anaesthetized patient who was never told about it, and a senior resident says 'everyone does this'. Which response best reflects the module's position?
options: Proceed, because a widespread practice is by definition acceptable
Proceed, because the exam does not compromise her surgical care
Decline: prevalence does not create consent, and the obligation to resist unethical practice holds even at personal cost
Proceed, but tell the patient afterwards
questions.explain: Why: the module's second scenario is built on exactly this pressure and its questions ask whether prevalence changes the ethics; its stated position is that "just following orders" is unacceptable and that students are obligated to resist unethical practice even in the face of personal consequences. Explicit consent had not been obtained. Not the others: each accepts the appeal to common practice or to lack of physical harm that the module rejects.

guide.s: explicit consent had not been obtained

questions.stem: A resident lists venlafaxine XR as a first-line agent for four disorders covered this week. For which of the following is it second line rather than first line?
questions.explain: Why: the OCD module places venlafaxine XR with clomipramine as second line behind five first-line SSRIs. Not the others: venlafaxine XR is first line in social anxiety disorder, GAD and PTSD.

questions.stem: Which pairing of drug and the only disorder on whose first-line list it appears this week is correct?
questions.explain: Why: duloxetine is named for GAD only. Not the others: fluvoxamine is on the social anxiety and OCD lists, never GAD; pregabalin is social anxiety and GAD, not OCD; propranolol PRN is for performance-only social anxiety, not the generalized form.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman avoids buses, cinemas and queues because she fears she could not get out if she panicked; she is comfortable giving presentations. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explain: Why: fear of two or more of public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, crowds or queues, and being out alone, driven by the thought that escape would be difficult, is agoraphobia. Not the others: she has no fear of evaluation; the fear spans several situation types rather than one object; there is no generalized worry.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man reports four months of 'racing thoughts' about money and his health, lies awake making lists, is exhausted by day, is irritable and tense, and denies feeling special or doing anything out of character. Which feature most reliably steers away from a manic or hypomanic episode?
options: Daytime exhaustion despite poor sleep, rather than reduced need for sleep with preserved energy
questions.explain: Why: in mania sleep is reduced but energy is preserved; worry-driven insomnia leaves the person tired. With no grandiosity and no uncharacteristic behaviour, the picture is GAD. Not the others: four months does not exclude bipolar disorder; irritability occurs in both; situational fast speech is not pressured speech.

questions.stem: A patient with OCD reports that hand-washing gives instant relief but the urge returns just as strong. Their therapist shows two graphs. Which description matches the curve for exposure with response prevention?
options: An abrupt drop to baseline with the same peak every time
Progressively lower peaks that come down sooner, settling on a common low plateau
A steadily rising baseline across sessions
No change in peak but a longer time to recover
questions.explain: Why: exposure without the ritual produces habituation: each successive peak is lower and resolves sooner, because the feared consequence does not occur. Not the others: the abrupt drop with an unchanged peak is the compulsion curve, which maintains the disorder through negative reinforcement.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly orders the typical age of onset from earliest to latest as the modules give it?
options: GAD, OCD, social anxiety disorder, PTSD
Social anxiety disorder, OCD, PTSD, GAD
OCD, social anxiety disorder, GAD, PTSD
PTSD, GAD, OCD, social anxiety disorder
questions.explain: Why: social anxiety disorder has a median onset of 13, OCD a mean of 19.5, PTSD mid-to-late twenties, and GAD a median of 30, the latest of the anxiety disorders. Not the others: each misplaces at least one disorder.

guide.s: Social anxiety starts in early adolescence

questions.stem: A student recalls that a lifetime prevalence of about 9% was quoted for two disorders this week and that 1 to 3% belongs to a third. Which set is correct?
options: 9%: social anxiety disorder and PTSD; 2–3%: GAD
questions.explain: Why: GAD 9% and PTSD 9% (quiz band 6–9%) share the figure; OCD is 2–3%, and 1–3% is the planted distractor on the PTSD item. Not the others: no lifetime percentage is given for social anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has had five days of elevated mood, sleeping three hours without fatigue, talking rapidly and starting several projects; she is still attending classes and completing her work, and there are no psychotic features. Which is the best characterization?
questions.explain: Why: at least four days of elevated mood with increased energy and no marked functional impairment, no psychosis and no hospitalization is a hypomanic episode. Not the others: mania requires a week or marked impairment; cyclothymia requires two years of subthreshold swings; preserved energy on three hours of sleep is the opposite of GAD's fatigue.

questions.stem: A patient starting lithium asks how the dose will be chosen and what to expect. Which answer is correct?
options: A weight-based dose, with liver enzymes checked monthly
A dose titrated to trough serum levels, with a fine tremor as a common expected effect
A standard loading dose, with osteoporosis screening
A dose set by hepatic function, with vitiligo as a common effect
questions.explain: Why: lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is titrated to serum levels; it is renally cleared, so hepatic function is irrelevant; a fine tremor is a common counselling point, and a coarse tremor signals toxicity. Not the others: weight-based dosing, loading protocols, osteoporosis and vitiligo are not part of lithium initiation; fatty liver belongs to valproate.

questions.stem: A patient reports two weeks of poor sleep, low energy, poor concentration, weight loss and guilt, but denies low mood and still enjoys her usual activities. Why do these five symptoms not satisfy the criteria for a major depressive episode?
options: Because at least one of depressed mood or anhedonia must be present
Because the duration must be four weeks
Because weight loss is not a criterion
questions.explain: Why: the rule is at least five of nine, one of which must be depressed mood or anhedonia; five non-core symptoms do not qualify. Not the others: five is the count; two weeks is the duration; weight change is a criterion.

questions.stem: A patient with social anxiety says, 'I froze once in a meeting, so I always make a fool of myself and I'm a complete failure.' Which two distortions are illustrated, in order?
questions.explain: Why: turning one event into an always rule is overgeneralization; attaching a global negative identity, "a complete failure", is labeling. Not the others: nothing positive is explained away and no future catastrophe is predicted.

questions.stem: Which statement about how medication and psychotherapy compare is correct according to the modules?
options: In specific phobia, SSRIs and CBT are equally effective
In GAD, pharmacological and psychological treatments have equivalent efficacy
In OCD, medication alone is superior to CBT alone
In PTSD, benzodiazepines are the first-line drug
questions.explain: Why: the GAD module states equivalent efficacy for medication and therapy, and the quiz keys CBT plus an SSRI as most effective. Not the others: specific phobia has little evidence for any medication; in OCD CBT is equal or superior, and CBT plus medication beats medication alone but not CBT alone; in PTSD the first line is an antidepressant and the benzodiazepine option is keyed wrong.

guide.s: CBT plus medication beats medication alone

cards.prompt: What proportion of Canadians will meet criteria for a mood or anxiety disorder in their lifetime, and for any mental health or substance use disorder?
cards.answer: Mood or anxiety disorder: 1 in 5 (about 21.3%). Any mental health or substance use disorder: 1 in 3.

cards.text: Burnout is a syndrome of {{emotional exhaustion}}, {{depersonalization}} and a low sense of {{personal accomplishment}}, developing in response to enduring work-related stress.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are risk factors for burnout named by the module?
What proportion of healthcare trainees and professionals report burnout?
What is the module's discriminator between burnout and depression?
cards.answer: Burnout's negative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are tied to work and improve away from work; depression's are pervasive and persistent across contexts and time.

cards.prompt: Place the module's continuum in order from its starting point to its endpoint.
items: Stress
Burnout
Depression
Suicidality

cards.prompt: Match each figure to the population and measure it describes.
pairs: Medical students with depression or depressive symptoms
US residents with depression or depressive symptoms
Canadian residents with a positive depression screen
Depressed medical students who sought treatment

cards.prompt: Match each source to what it studied.
pairs: Depression and depressive symptoms among resident physicians
Depression and suicidal ideation among medical students
Burnout, depression screen and suicidal ideation in Canadian residents
Background review for the anxiety self-learning modules

cards.prompt: Which of the following are among the module's six barriers to medical trainees seeking mental health treatment?
options: More unwanted licensing or supervision oversight

guide.s: lower rates of depression and burnout

cards.prompt: Compared with similar-aged peers, students accepted to medical school have which pattern of depression and burnout before training begins?
Which of the following does the module list as system-level consequences of burnout?

guide.s: most common mental health disorder in women

cards.prompt: Where does specific phobia rank among mental disorders in women and in men?
cards.answer: Most common mental health disorder in women; second most common in men, behind substance-related disorders.

cards.text: In specific phobia the phobic object {{almost always}} provokes immediate fear, is actively avoided or {{endured with intense fear}}, and the fear typically lasts {{six months}} or more.

cards.prompt: Match each feared stimulus to its DSM-5 specifier.
Which specifiers does the module name as the most common specific phobias?
What is the gold-standard treatment for specific phobia, and what is the evidence for medication?
cards.answer: CBT with exposure (systematic desensitization). Little evidence supports medication in most cases; the module names no drug.

cards.prompt: Put the steps of systematic desensitization in order.
items: Rank fears on a hierarchy from 1 to 10, with 10 the most feared
Start graded exposure at the lowest level, paired with relaxation techniques
Once desensitized at that level, move up to the next level

cards.prompt: Order the module's spider-phobia hierarchy from least to most feared.
items: Look at a picture of a spider
Hold a rubber spider
Look at a live spider in a jar
Touch the jar containing the spider
Stand two feet from a live spider
Touch a live spider

cards.prompt: A fear driven by anticipated negative evaluation by others points to which diagnosis rather than specific phobia?
In the module's case, what specifier applies to Stuart, and which feature of his history makes the fear a disorder rather than a dislike?
cards.answer: Situational (airplanes). Occupational impairment: he is considering declining a promotion because of the fear.

cards.text: Social anxiety disorder is the {{second}} most common anxiety disorder, with a median age of onset of {{13}} and 75% beginning between ages {{7 and 15}}.

cards.prompt: What is the core fear in social anxiety disorder (criterion B)?
cards.answer: Fear of acting in a way, or showing anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated by others.

cards.prompt: Which disorders does criterion I name as ones that must not better explain the presentation?
Which medical conditions does criterion J give as examples, and what must be true of the fear for the diagnosis to stand?
cards.answer: Parkinson's disease, obesity, and disfigurement from burns or injury. The fear must be clearly unrelated to the condition or excessive.

cards.prompt: When does the performance-only specifier apply, and what does it change about treatment?
cards.answer: When the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public. Treatment becomes propranolol as needed rather than a daily SSRI, venlafaxine XR or pregabalin.

cards.prompt: Match each first-line agent to its class on the module's flowchart.
Which SSRIs are named on the social anxiety disorder first-line flowchart?
Which two entries on the social anxiety differential appear on neither the specific phobia nor the GAD differential, and which non-disorder opens the list?
cards.answer: Selective mutism and avoidant personality disorder. The list opens with normative shyness.

cards.prompt: Which of these does the module give as examples of avoidance in social anxiety disorder?
What are the two named components of CBT for social anxiety disorder, and why does the module call CBT the gold-standard non-pharmacological treatment rather than simply the gold standard?
cards.answer: Cognitive techniques (restructuring and challenging maladaptive thoughts) and behavioural techniques (exposures). Because, unlike specific phobia, social anxiety disorder also has a first-line drug list.

cards.text: GAD requires excessive worry more days than not for at least {{six months}} about a number of events, which the person finds {{difficult to control}}, with {{three}} or more of six associated symptoms.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are among the six associated symptoms of GAD in the module?
Give GAD's lifetime prevalence, median age of onset, sex ratio, and rate of comorbid major depressive disorder.
cards.answer: 9% lifetime; median onset 30 (latest of the anxiety disorders, rarely before adolescence); females 2:1; comorbid MDD in up to 50%.

cards.prompt: Match each excluded diagnosis to the module's reason for excluding it in Peter's case.
pairs: No recurrent unexpected panic attacks; worry is generalized
A pervasive personality pattern of orderliness, perfectionism and control

cards.prompt: Which two medical conditions does the GAD module name as causes of anxiety to rule out, and which substance is its worked example?
cards.answer: Pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism. Caffeine.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are on the GAD module's list of psychological treatments?
Which two therapies does the module recommend most for GAD, and what is the stated purpose of psychoeducation?
cards.answer: CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. Psychoeducation aims to prevent avoidance of anxiety triggers.

cards.prompt: Which agents are first line for GAD in the module?
Which drug class does the module key as having the most evidence for treating GAD?
Which four SSRI side effects does the GAD module list?
cards.answer: GI symptoms, headaches, weight gain and sexual dysfunction (all of the above).

cards.prompt: Match each drink to its caffeine content per serving on the module's infographic.
Compare the median ages of onset of social anxiety disorder and GAD.
cards.answer: Social anxiety disorder: median 13, 75% between 7 and 15. GAD: median 30, very unlikely before adolescence, the latest-onset anxiety disorder.

guide.s: occupy more than one hour a day

cards.text: OCD criterion B requires marked distress, symptoms occupying more than {{one hour}} a day, or significant interference with {{functioning}}.

cards.prompt: Give OCD's lifetime prevalence, mean age of onset, and the rate in first-degree relatives.
cards.answer: Lifetime prevalence 2–3%; mean onset 19.5 years (earlier peak in males); about 10% of first-degree relatives affected. It is the WHO's tenth leading cause of disability and runs a chronic course.

cards.prompt: Match each obsessive thought to its corresponding rituals in the module's matching exercise.
pairs: Ordering, arranging, placing objects just so

cards.prompt: What are the OCD specifiers in DSM-5 as the module presents them?
cards.answer: Insight: with good or fair insight, with poor insight, or with absent insight/delusional beliefs. And tic-related, if there is a current or past tic disorder.

cards.prompt: Match each related disorder to its discriminating feature.
pairs: Obsessions and compulsions limited to physical appearance
Exclusively difficulty discarding and excessive accumulation
Hair pulling in the absence of obsessions
Enduring perfectionism and rigid control without intrusions

cards.prompt: How does the module distinguish a complex tic from a compulsion?
cards.answer: Compulsions are usually preceded by obsessions; tics are often preceded by premonitory sensory urges. Tics are less complex and not aimed at neutralizing obsessions; both diagnoses may be given.

cards.prompt: Which agents are first line for OCD in the module?
Which two agents does the module name as popular second-line options for OCD?
cards.answer: Clomipramine (a tricyclic) and venlafaxine XR (an SNRI).

cards.text: In OCD the treatment goal is {{improvement}} rather than remission; doses start low and aim {{high}}; response often takes {{6–12}} weeks; an adequate trial requires {{12–15}} weeks; treatment continues for at least {{one year}}.

cards.prompt: Put the steps of exposure and response prevention in order.
items: Define a range of obsessional triggers
Rank the degree of discomfort with each trigger
Build a hierarchy with the most distressing trigger at the top
Expose the patient systematically to each trigger while preventing rituals and avoidance

cards.prompt: Which of the following are components of CBT for OCD in the module?
Which is listed as a distinctive advantage of medication over CBT for OCD in the module's comparison table?

cards.text: PTSD requires at least {{one}} intrusion symptom, {{one}} avoidance symptom, {{two}} negative cognition or mood symptoms and {{two}} arousal symptoms, lasting more than {{one month}}.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are routes of trauma exposure named by the module?
options: Learning it happened to a loved one

cards.prompt: Which of the following are intrusion symptoms in the module's PTSD criteria?
Which of the following are arousal and reactivity symptoms in the module's PTSD criteria?
Give PTSD's lifetime prevalence, sex ratio, typical onset, most common trauma source and effect on suicide risk.
cards.answer: Lifetime prevalence 9% (quiz band 6–9%); twice as common in females; onset mid-to-late twenties (25–30); sexual or relationship violence is the most common trauma; suicide risk increased two- to three-fold.

cards.prompt: Which of the following does the module list as PTSD risk factors?
What single axis does the module use to distinguish acute stress disorder from PTSD, and what is the expected course of acute stress disorder?
cards.answer: Time: acute stress disorder is symptoms within the first 30 days; PTSD is a disturbance lasting over one month. Most patients with acute stress disorder recover; a subset persist and are diagnosed with PTSD.

cards.prompt: Match each therapy to the module's description.
pairs: Psychoeducation, relaxation, cognitive processing, trauma narrative, mastery of reminders
Rhythmic movements or sounds while processing trauma memories
Gradual confrontation of trauma memories, feelings and situations

cards.prompt: Which therapy does the module key as most effective for PTSD, and which does it key for Annie when trauma-focused CBT is not offered?
cards.answer: Most effective and mainstay: trauma-focused CBT. For Annie from a list without TF-CBT: EMDR, the only trauma-processing therapy offered.

cards.prompt: Which agents are first line for PTSD in the module?
How is venlafaxine XR positioned in the PTSD and OCD modules respectively?
options: First line in PTSD, second line in OCD
Second line in PTSD, first line in OCD

cards.text: In 2013 there were over {{4,000}} suicides in Canada; suicide was the {{ninth}} leading cause of death overall and the {{second}} leading cause at ages 15 to 24, with the highest rates at ages {{40 to 59}}.

cards.prompt: State the sex difference in suicide attempts and deaths.
cards.answer: Females are three to four times more likely to attempt suicide; males are more likely to die by suicide.

cards.prompt: Match each letter of SAD PERSONS to its item.

cards.text: SAD PERSONS: Sex (male), Age (under 20 or over {{45}}), Depression, Previous attempts, {{Ethanol}} or substance use, Rational thinking loss, {{Social supports}} lacking, Organized plan, No spouse, Sickness or pain.

cards.prompt: Match each risk factor to the category the module places it in.
Which single risk factor does the module call one of the most powerful predictors of suicide for all age groups?
cards.answer: A history of previous suicide attempts. Always ask about prior attempts.

cards.prompt: According to the module, does asking a patient about suicide increase their risk?
options: Yes, it can plant the idea
No; the real barrier is the clinician's own discomfort
Only if asked more than once

cards.prompt: Put the module's four assessment steps in order.
items: Assess current suicidal plan and intent
Assess the intensity of the suicidal thinking
Assess risk factors (SAD PERSONS)
Assess reasons for living and protective factors

cards.prompt: Distinguish passive from active suicidal thoughts as the module defines them.
cards.answer: Passive: a wish to be dead or never to wake up. Active: a specific plan, such as jumping from a height, hanging, or overdosing.

cards.prompt: Which of the following belong to the module's assessment of the intensity of suicidal thinking?
options: Arrangements such as a note or a will

cards.prompt: Which of the following are protective factors listed by the module?
What defines a mental disorder due to another medical condition, and what does the definition explicitly exclude?
cards.answer: Psychiatric symptoms that are a direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition and improve when it is treated. It excludes psychosocial reactions to having the illness.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are among criteria B to E for a disorder due to another medical condition?
options: Evidence from history, examination or laboratory findings of a direct pathophysiological consequence
Not better explained by another mental disorder
Symptoms present for at least two weeks
Does not occur exclusively during a delirium
At least five of nine symptoms

cards.prompt: Criterion E is satisfied by any one of which three things?
cards.answer: Clinically significant distress or impairment; hospitalization necessitated to prevent harm to self or others; or the presence of psychotic features.

cards.prompt: Match each disorder due to another medical condition to its criterion A.
pairs: Prominent, persistent depressed mood or markedly diminished interest predominating
Prominent, persistent elevated, expansive or irritable mood and increased activity or energy predominating
Panic attacks or anxiety predominant in the clinical picture

cards.prompt: Match each scenario to whether the module classes it as a direct pathophysiological consequence.
pairs: Panic attacks remitting after pheochromocytoma excision
Low mood two days after an MCA stroke
No: psychological reaction to a symptom
Hopelessness four weeks after a cancer diagnosis
No: reaction to the diagnosis; the tumour predated it

cards.prompt: Match each competing explanation to the criterion that excludes it.
pairs: C: not better explained by another mental disorder
B fails: no direct pathophysiological consequence
B: the cause is the drug, so medication-induced

cards.prompt: How does the module define delirium, and how does it relate to the diagnosis?
cards.answer: Rapid-onset, fluctuating changes in attention and orientation in the acutely ill. Symptoms occurring only during delirium are not a disorder due to another medical condition.

cards.prompt: Match each pathway to depression in HIV/AIDS with the diagnosis it produces.
pairs: Effect of the virus on the CNS
Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
Effect of antiretrovirals on the CNS

cards.text: Diagnosing a disorder due to another medical condition rests on {{time course}} (onset, exacerbation or remission with the condition), {{atypical features}} such as onset of panic at age 70, and a known or plausible {{pathophysiological mechanism}}.

cards.prompt: Which conditions does the module list as inducing anxiety symptoms?
Which two medications does the module name as inducing psychiatric symptoms?
cards.answer: Prednisone and antiretrovirals.

cards.prompt: What did the Nazi doctor Fritz Klein say when asked how he reconciled his oath with killing, and what does the module draw from it?
cards.answer: That out of respect for human life he would remove a gangrenous appendix, and 'the Jew is the gangrenous appendix in the body of mankind'. The oath was reinterpreted through a medical metaphor, not abandoned.

cards.text: During the Holocaust {{11 million}} civilian non-combatants were murdered, including {{6 million}} Jews, {{250,000}} people with disabilities and {{200,000}} Roma.

cards.prompt: What proportion of German doctors joined the Nazi party early, and how does the module characterize their support?
cards.answer: More than half were early joining members; the German Medical Association documented support for the Nazi agenda without coercion.

cards.prompt: Order the escalation the module describes physicians leading.
items: Sterilization of hundreds of thousands with 'hereditary diseases'
Systematic euthanasia of disabled children and the mentally ill
Industrialized genocide in extermination camps

cards.prompt: Which roles did physicians play in the death camps according to the module?
options: Selecting who was sent to the gas chambers and who to labour camps

cards.prompt: What is the Nuremberg Code, how many conditions does it set, and which three does the module name?
cards.answer: The first generally accepted code governing research on human subjects, produced after the 1946 Doctors' Trial (20 of 23 defendants physicians). Ten conditions; the module names informed consent, avoiding unnecessary mental or physical harm, and the right to withdraw consent at any time.

cards.prompt: Match each milestone to its year.
pairs: Tuskegee study ends after a whistleblower
Alberta Sexual Sterilization Act in force

cards.prompt: What was Syndrome K?
cards.answer: A fictional diagnosis invented by Dr. Adriano Ossicini at Fatebenefratelli Hospital in Rome in 1943 to mark healthy Jews who needed hiding; the 'patients' coughed to simulate TB during Nazi inspections, and dozens were saved.

cards.prompt: Which two features does the module say the medical profession shares with the Nazi regime, making physicians vulnerable to 'following orders'?
cards.answer: A culture of conformity and deference to hierarchy, and an ethical imperative to help that can be redirected.

cards.prompt: Where was intergenerational trauma first recognized, and how can it manifest in descendants?
cards.answer: In Holocaust survivors and their descendants; children and grandchildren of genocide survivors can show complex PTSD. It is now recognized in descendants of other genocides, of enslaved people, and of Indigenous Peoples.

cards.text: The Tuskegee study ran from {{1932}} to 1972, enrolled {{600}} Black men in Alabama who were told they had '{{bad blood}}', and withheld penicillin although it was standard by {{1947}}.

cards.prompt: What tuberculosis mortality figure does the module give for some residential schools, and what was the physicians' role?
cards.answer: Up to 70% of children died of TB alone at some schools in the early 1900s. Doctors did not intervene to prevent children with TB from being forcibly removed into those schools; later, physicians ran nutrition experiments on hundreds of children from six schools.

cards.prompt: What survey data does the module give on educational pelvic examinations under anaesthesia?
cards.answer: In 2003, 90% of 400 Philadelphia medical students surveyed had performed one; at the University of Oklahoma a large majority had, but only about a quarter of patients had consented.

Give patients a more active role in decisions
Increase moral concern and individualize patients

First line in social anxiety and GAD
First line SAD, GAD, PTSD; second line OCD

cards.prompt: Which SSRIs are on the first-line list for PTSD?
Which disorder this week has no first-line drug, and what is its treatment?
cards.answer: Specific phobia: little evidence supports medication in most cases. CBT with systematic desensitization is the gold standard: rank fears 1 to 10, start at 1/10, pair graded exposure with relaxation, advance once desensitized.

cards.prompt: Match each therapy to the disorder it is named for.
Contrast the anxiety curve after a compulsion with the curve across repeated exposures with response prevention.
cards.answer: Compulsion: abrupt drop straight back to baseline with the peak unchanged next time (negative reinforcement; disorder maintained). Exposure with response prevention: progressively lower peaks that resolve sooner, settling onto one low plateau (habituation).

cards.answer: Maintain a regular sleep cycle: sleep loss is both a prodromal sign and a precipitant of mania.
