guides.title: Week 41 · 1 Wellness in Medicine & the Burden of Mood and Anxiety Disorders
guides.html:
Pre-week · PW01 · PW02

Wellness in Medicine & the Burden of Mood and Anxiety Disorders

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How common mood and anxiety disorders are, why physicians are at higher risk, and what burnout is, costs, and hides behind.

How common mood and anxiety disorders are

Two Statistics Canada figures frame the week. One in three Canadians will meet criteria for a mental health or substance use disorder in their lifetime. Within that, one in five (about 21.3%) will meet criteria for a mood or anxiety disorder. The two numbers nest: the first is any disorder, the second is mood or anxiety specifically.

Mood and anxiety disorders carry a major impact on morbidity and mortality, and unrecognized they impair recovery from any other medical condition — the argument for every specialty, not only psychiatry. Teaching of these topics at UofT began in 2013; the strand on physicians' own mental health was added at students' request, on the premise that health care providers are more at risk than the rest of the population across medical school, residency and staff practice.

The pre-week package sets ten objectives in three blocks: one on the medical profession itself; a bipolar block of five (clinical features by DSM-5 criteria → differential diagnosis → psychosocial impact → biopsychosocial treatment → pharmacology); and an anxiety block of four on the same ladder, with clinical features covering anxiety disorders, OCD and PTSD together. Both pharmacology objectives ask for mechanism of action and common or serious side effects, not drug names alone.

The assigned pre-week items
Four items, in order: the Wellness in Medicine module (below); two video lectures by Dr. Jason Quinn on bipolar and related disorders — Diagnosis and Psychosocial Impact (20:35) and Treatment (12:59); and the background review for the anxiety modules, Craske and Stein, Anxiety, Lancet 2016. The optional guidelines (Katzman 2014 on anxiety, PTSD and OCD; CANMAT/ISBD 2018 on bipolar disorder; ISBD 2009 on safety monitoring; CANMAT 2016 on depression) are explicitly excluded from the Mastery Exercise.

The evidence the wellness module rests on is named in the package: two JAMA meta-analyses — Mata et al. 2015 on depression and depressive symptoms in resident physicians, and Rotenstein et al. 2016 on medical students, which also measured suicidal ideation — plus Canadian data from the CMA. The reflective hook is Michelle's story and the ways the medical system creates barriers to trainees and physicians seeking help.

Burnout: the definition

Burnout is a syndrome of three dimensions, after Maslach:

  1. Emotional exhaustion
  2. Depersonalization
  3. Low sense of personal accomplishment

It develops in response to enduring work-related stress and leads to decreased effectiveness at work. The definition is anchored to work, which is what later separates it from depression.

When it happens

Five risk factors, all occupational: high workload, low sense of control, low autonomy, seemingly endless or meaningless work, and work–life imbalance. All five are common features of medical training, and the resulting prevalence is 24–54% of healthcare trainees and professionals reporting burnout. The module gives no individual-level predisposing factors; the risk lives in the structure of the work.

What burnout costs

Individual consequencesSystem consequences
Loss of empathyPoor quality care
AbsenteeismPatient dissatisfaction
QuittingIncreased medical errors
Relationship problemsIncreased malpractice litigation
Family problemsIncreased hospital-associated infections
Health problemsIncreased patient mortality

The two columns are independent lists, not matched pairs. The system column escalates from soft outcomes to hard ones, ending in hospital-associated infections and patient mortality — the consequences of burnout fall on patients as well as on the person burning out.

Burnout and depression

Burnout may precede or precipitate depression, and the module frames it as a modifiable risk and aggravating factor for depression. The pathway is drawn as a continuum: stress → burnout → depression → suicidality, with burnout the way-station between ordinary stress and illness. The summary slide states it more strongly: burnout leads to increased risk of depression and suicidality.

BurnoutDepression
Improves away from workNegative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are pervasive and persistent
Negative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are associated with workPresent across contexts and over time
The discriminator is context: a resident who is cynical and depleted on service but well on a two-week holiday has burnout; a resident who is anhedonic on holiday too has depression.

The numbers

The order of the evidence matters. Before training, students accepted to medical school have lower rates of depression and burnout than similar-aged peers. Stress during medical school then raises the risk of both. Because matriculants start better off and end up worse, the excess distress is attributable to training rather than to who chooses medicine.

PopulationMeasureFigure
Healthcare trainees and professionalsReport burnout24–54%
Medical studentsDepression or depressive symptoms27%
General population, 18–25Depression9.3%
General population, 26–49Depression7.2%
Medical studentsRise in depressive symptoms after training begins13.5%
Medical studentsSuicidal ideation, past two weeks to a year11% (past two weeks 7.4%; past year 24.4%)
US residentsDepression or depressive symptoms21–43%
US residentsMedian absolute increase in depressive symptoms within a year of starting residency16%
Canadian residents (CMA national survey, 2018)Burnout38%
Canadian residentsPositive depression screen48%
Canadian residentsSuicidal ideation, past year15%
Medical students screening positive for depressionSought psychiatric or mental health treatment15.7%

Three sets are easily confused: the medical-student figures (27% depression; 11% suicidal ideation), the US resident figures (21–43%; a 16% increase in the first year), and the Canadian resident figures from the CMA survey (38% burnout, 48% depression screen, 15% suicidal ideation). The student depression rate of 27% is roughly three to four times the general-population rates of 9.3% and 7.2%. The suicidal-ideation sub-figures are printed as the module prints them, with the past-year figure larger than the pooled headline.

The treatment gap and why it exists

Of medical students who screen positive for depression, 15.7% seek psychiatric or mental health treatment — roughly one in six, leaving about 84% untreated. The module's answer to why is a list of six barriers converging on a single construct:

  1. Lack of time
  2. Cost
  3. Confidentiality concerns
  4. Potential career implications
  5. Exposure to unwanted interventions
  6. More unwanted licensing or supervision oversight

The first two are practical; the other four are consequences specific to being a trainee in medicine. All six drain into stigma, framed with the module's irony: mental health conditions are heavily stigmatized in the medical profession even though physicians long fought to have them classified as medical diagnoses.

Michelle's story
The module's one interactive item is an ungraded reflection: a video of a trainee's account, followed by the prompt to identify reasons medical trainees may not seek care. The intended answers are the barriers above and the stigma beneath them; there is no keyed response.

Resources named

UofT Medicine Wellness · 10 TED Talks for When You Feel Burnt Out · the Provider Resilience app for burnout · MoodGym, a CBT website for depression · Sleepio, a CBT website for insomnia and depression. Three of the five are self-directed e-health tools, matching the module's cited evidence on web-based tools for burnout, depression and suicidality among health professionals.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • One in three is any mental health or substance use disorder; one in five (21.3%) is a mood or anxiety disorder. Reversing them is the common error.
  • Burnout has three dimensions, not two: exhaustion, depersonalization and low accomplishment. Cynicism alone is not the definition.
  • 24–54% is trainees and professionals together; 27% is medical students; 38% is Canadian residents. Each figure belongs to one population.
  • Selection does not explain the excess: entrants are healthier than peers before training starts.
  • Burnout improves away from work; depression does not. A vignette turns on whether symptoms lift on holiday.
  • Mata 2015 = residents; Rotenstein 2016 = students plus suicidal ideation.
  • The module names no treatment for burnout and no protective factors; a question asking what the module recommends for burnout has no supported answer beyond the resources list.
Modifiable is the load-bearing word. Burnout is presented as a modifiable risk factor for depression, which is the module's argument for institutional intervention. An option that treats burnout as a fixed personal trait, or as equivalent to depression, is wrong on the module's own terms.
One in five Canadians will have a mood or anxiety disorder; physicians are at higher risk at every career stage, and training itself raises it. Burnout is a three-part, work-bound syndrome that improves away from work, sits between stress and depression on a continuum, costs patients as well as clinicians, and goes untreated in most depressed medical students because six barriers converge on stigma.

guides.title: Week 41 · 2 Specific Phobia
guides.html:
SLM01 · Anxiety

Specific Phobia

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Criteria, stimulus specifiers, the differential, and why graded exposure rather than medication is the treatment.

The case: Stuart, 45, afraid of flying

A 45-year-old stockbroker on Bay Street, married with two children, has just been promoted into a role that requires flying from Toronto to Alberta and British Columbia several times a month. He is considering turning the promotion down because of a significant fear of flying. For years he has driven or taken the train to meetings instead — including driving from Toronto to Los Angeles each year for the annual general meeting. No psychiatric or medical history; lorazepam 2 mg as needed for anxiety; no substance use; his mother had severe agoraphobia; he is outgoing with a close network of supports.

The case maps onto the criteria without the module saying so: the feared situation is flying (criterion A); the loudest feature is active avoidance, driving across the continent rather than boarding a plane (C); and occupational impairment — a promotion at risk — is what turns a dislike of flying into a disorder (F). The specifier is situational. Three details are there to mislead: the outgoing personality and strong supports argue against social anxiety disorder; the mother's agoraphobia is family loading, but agoraphobia is itself on the differential; and the as-needed lorazepam is a realistic community prescription that the module's own pharmacology slide does not support.

Epidemiology

Specific phobia is the most common mental health disorder in women and the second most common in men, behind substance-related disorders. It is commonly comorbid with other anxiety disorders, mood disorders and substance-related disorders. The module gives no prevalence percentage, age of onset or sex ratio; those two sentences are the whole epidemiology, and both are repeated in the summary.

DSM-5 criteria

All seven are required.

Criterion
AMarked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation (flying, heights, animals, receiving an injection, seeing blood)
BThe phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety
CThe phobic object or situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety
DThe fear or anxiety is out of proportion to the actual danger posed and to the sociocultural context
EThe fear, anxiety or avoidance is persistent, typically lasting six months or more
FIt causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of function
GNot better explained by symptoms of another mental disorder

Three details of wording carry exam weight. Criterion B says almost always, not always, so a patient who manages the occasional exposure still meets it. Criterion C allows endurance with intense fear as well as avoidance: the passenger who white-knuckles the flight still qualifies. The only number in the set is the six-month duration, which is the same duration threshold used for social anxiety disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.

Specifiers: the phobic stimulus

SpecifierExamples
AnimalInsects, spiders, dogs
Natural environmentHeights, storms, water
Blood-injection-injuryNeedles, invasive medical procedures
SituationalAirplanes, elevators, enclosed spaces
OtherChoking, vomiting, loud noises, costumed characters

The summary names the four most common phobia types as animals, natural environments, blood-injection-injury and situational; other is a valid specifier but is not claimed to be common. The pairing most often tested is the odd one: a fear of clowns is other, not situational.

Differential diagnosis

The module lists nine possibilities in this order: agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, separation anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, trauma- and stressor-related disorders, eating disorders, psychotic disorders, and other medical conditions or substances. It gives no discriminators of its own; the organizing question is what exactly is feared, and what makes the fear stop.

DiagnosisWhat drives the fear or avoidance
Specific phobiaOne circumscribed object or situation; immediate fear on exposure
Social anxiety disorderFear of negative evaluation by others
AgoraphobiaFear of being unable to escape or get help, across multiple situation types
Separation anxiety disorderFear of separation from an attachment figure
Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected panic attacks not tied to one cue
Obsessive-compulsive disorderAvoidance driven by an obsession
Trauma- and stressor-related disordersAvoidance of trauma reminders
Eating disordersAvoidance of food driven by weight or shape concern
Psychotic disordersAvoidance driven by a delusion

Only the social-anxiety and panic discriminators come from this week's own modules; the rest are standard psychiatry. The final item on the list, ruling out medical conditions and substances, appears in all three anxiety modules.

Treatment

Cognitive behavioural therapy

CBT is the gold-standard treatment for specific phobia. It works by exposure to the feared stimulus, in the module's terms systematic desensitization. The CBT triangle behind it — thoughts, feelings and behaviours joined by bidirectional arrows — is the justification for treating a phobia behaviourally: changing behaviour through exposure changes the thoughts and feelings, rather than the patient being argued out of the belief.

Systematic desensitization

  1. The person ranks their fears on a hierarchy from 1 to 10, with 10 the most feared.
  2. Exposure starts at the lowest level, with graded exposures paired with relaxation techniques.
  3. Once the person is desensitized at that level, exposure moves up to the next; progression is criterion-based, not time-based.
Spider hierarchyFear level
Look at a picture of a spider1/10
Hold a rubber spider3/10
Look at a live spider in a jar5/10
Touch the jar containing the spider8/10
Stand two feet from a live spider9/10
Touch a live spider10/10

The hierarchy climbs along two axes at once, representational to real and distance to contact, and its biggest jump (5 to 8) comes at the first physical contact with the container. Starting at the bottom is what makes this graded exposure rather than flooding.

Medication

There is little evidence to support medication in specific phobia in most cases; the module's image is a pile of pills under a prohibition sign. No drug is named anywhere in the module. Specific phobia is the one anxiety disorder in this week's set with no first-line drug, which is the contrast to hold against social anxiety disorder (a full first-line flowchart) and GAD (three drug classes).

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Impairment is the diagnostic hinge. A dislike of flying becomes a disorder when a promotion is at stake.
  • Endured with intense fear counts. Boarding the plane in terror still satisfies criterion C.
  • Six months is the duration, shared with social anxiety disorder and GAD.
  • Clown = other, elevator = situational, needle = blood-injection-injury, storm = natural environment.
  • Most common disorder in women, second in men, with substance-related disorders first in men.
  • CBT with graded exposure is the answer to every treatment question; a medication option, including the patient's own as-needed benzodiazepine, is not supported.
  • A fear of multiple public situations with no escape is agoraphobia; a fear of being judged is social anxiety disorder; neither is a specific phobia even when a single situation dominates the story.
The benzodiazepine in the case is not the module's recommendation. Stuart arrives on lorazepam 2 mg as needed; two sections later the module says medications have little evidence in specific phobia and CBT is the gold standard. A question asking for the best treatment expects CBT, not continuation or optimization of the benzodiazepine.
Specific phobia is marked, immediate, out-of-proportion fear of one object or situation, avoided or endured, lasting six months or more and causing impairment. It is the commonest mental disorder in women, is specified by stimulus type, and is treated with CBT by graded exposure up a 1-to-10 hierarchy, with no first-line medication.

guides.title: Week 41 · 3 Social Anxiety Disorder
guides.html:
SLM02 · Anxiety

Social Anxiety Disorder

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Fear of negative evaluation: the ten criteria, the performance-only specifier, the differential, and the first-line drug flowchart.

The case: Lindsay, 23, presenting in class

A 23-year-old law student, single, family in Ottawa, has increasing anxiety about presenting in class. Before a presentation she gets tachycardia, shortness of breath, chest pain, chills, a choking sensation and a fear of losing control. She also avoids social gatherings because she fears she will do something embarrassing. History: a depressive episode in high school treated with fluoxetine; hyperthyroidism; an oral contraceptive; one or two shots of whisky before presentations "to calm her nerves" and no other alcohol or substance use; a father described as a worrier; a supportive family; shy throughout school.

The six somatic symptoms are panic-attack symptoms, placed so that the reader must choose between social anxiety disorder with panic attacks and panic disorder. Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks; Lindsay's are cued, arriving before presentations. Her stated fear of doing something embarrassing is the fear of negative evaluation at the core of the diagnosis. Because she avoids social gatherings as well as presentations, the performance-only specifier does not apply, which also decides her drug treatment. Three history items are differential traps rather than confirmations: hyperthyroidism is a medical cause of anxiety to rule out; the pre-presentation whisky is both a substance red flag and the classic self-medicating safety behaviour of social anxiety; and the past depressive episode puts major depressive disorder, which sits on the differential, in play. The module never states her diagnosis; the intended reading is social anxiety disorder, not performance-only.

Epidemiology

  • The second most common anxiety disorder, behind specific phobia.
  • Median age of onset 13; 75% begin between ages 7 and 15.
  • More common in females than males (no ratio given).
  • Impairs educational and occupational performance and family functioning, with reduced overall quality of life.
  • Highly comorbid, most commonly with major depressive disorder and other anxiety disorders.

The onset numbers are the ones the week's quizzes are built around: social anxiety disorder begins in early adolescence, median 13; GAD begins latest of the three, median 30, and very rarely before adolescence.

DSM-5 criteria

Ten lettered criteria, all required, plus one specifier.

Criterion
AMarked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations
BFear of acting in a way, or showing anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated
CThe social interactions almost always provoke fear or anxiety
DThe situations are avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety
EThe fear is out of proportion to the actual threat and to the sociocultural context
FPersistent, typically six months or more
GClinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas
HNot attributable to a substance or another medical condition
INot better explained by another mental disorder, such as panic disorder, body dysmorphic disorder or autism spectrum disorder
JIf another medical condition is present (Parkinson's disease, obesity, disfigurement from burns or injury), the fear is clearly unrelated or excessive
SpecifyPerformance only: the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public

Four wording points matter. One social situation is enough for criterion A; the number of situations decides the specifier, not the diagnosis. Criterion B is the disorder's core and best discriminator: the feared outcome is negative evaluation, including of the visible anxiety itself, which separates social anxiety from specific phobia (fear of the thing), agoraphobia (fear of not escaping) and panic disorder (fear of the attack). Criterion I names three rule-outs — panic disorder, body dysmorphic disorder, autism spectrum disorder. Criterion J handles a real disfigurement: fear proportionate to a visible condition is not the disorder; fear clearly unrelated or excessive still can be.

Criteria counts across the three anxiety modules
Specific phobia A–G, seven. Social anxiety disorder A–J, ten. GAD, as this course presents it, three statements with a three-of-six symptom count. All three share the six-month duration.

What avoidance looks like

The module's examples: avoiding parties, avoiding school, avoiding jobs that require social interaction, avoiding presentations, and avoiding eating in public. These map onto the impairment domains of criterion G. Eating in public is the item that separates social anxiety from an eating disorder on history: the fear is of being watched and judged while eating, not of the food or of weight.

Differential diagnosis

Twelve items in the module's order: normative shyness, agoraphobia, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, separation anxiety disorder, specific phobias, selective mutism, major depressive disorder, delusional disorder, autism spectrum disorder, avoidant personality disorder, and other medical conditions or substances.

The list opens with a non-disorder, and that is the first decision: whether the shyness is a disorder at all, settled by duration (F), impairment (G) and disproportion (E), not by the shyness itself. Selective mutism and avoidant personality disorder appear on no other module's list. Delusional disorder stands for avoidance driven by a delusion of being watched. GAD and social anxiety disorder each appear on the other's differential.

Treatment

Cognitive behavioural therapy

CBT is the gold-standard non-pharmacological treatment, with two named halves: cognitive techniques — restructuring and challenging maladaptive thoughts — and behavioural techniques — exposures. The word non-pharmacological is deliberate: unlike specific phobia, social anxiety disorder has a first-line drug list beside CBT. The module gives no exposure hierarchy of its own; the worked hierarchy is in the specific phobia module.

Pharmacotherapy: the first-line flowchart

PresentationClassAgents named
GeneralizedSSRIsEscitalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine
SNRIVenlafaxine XR
OtherPregabalin
Performance onlyBeta blockerPropranolol as needed, before the performance
  • Everything on the chart is first line; the module gives no second-line agent.
  • The generalized-versus-performance-only split drives the choice: a daily antidepressant or pregabalin for generalized fear, propranolol as needed for performance-only fear.
  • Fluvoxamine appears here and not in the GAD list; escitalopram, sertraline and paroxetine are first line in both; fluoxetine is in neither list and appears only as Lindsay's past antidepressant.
  • Pregabalin is the one non-antidepressant first-line agent in both social anxiety disorder and GAD.
  • No benzodiazepine is first line in either module.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Cued versus unexpected. Panic symptoms before presentations are social anxiety with panic attacks; recurrent unexpected attacks are panic disorder.
  • Negative evaluation is the core fear. Fear of the situation itself is specific phobia; fear of no escape is agoraphobia.
  • Performance only requires the fear to be restricted to speaking or performing in public. Avoiding parties as well rules the specifier out and moves treatment from propranolol to a daily agent.
  • Median onset 13, 75% between 7 and 15; GAD median onset 30.
  • Shy since childhood is not the diagnosis; six months, impairment and disproportion make it one.
  • Hyperthyroidism and pre-performance alcohol are the two history items that must be addressed before the label is settled.
  • Criterion I's named exclusions: panic disorder, body dysmorphic disorder, autism spectrum disorder. Criterion J's medical examples: Parkinson's disease, obesity, disfigurement.
Propranolol is as-needed and performance-only. It is not a daily treatment and not an option for generalized social anxiety. A stem describing avoidance of parties, school or eating in public expects an SSRI, venlafaxine XR or pregabalin, not a beta blocker.
Social anxiety disorder is fear of negative evaluation in one or more social situations, almost always provoked, avoided or endured, disproportionate, six months or more, and impairing. It begins around age 13, is second only to specific phobia among anxiety disorders, and is treated with CBT plus, for generalized fear, an SSRI, venlafaxine XR or pregabalin; propranolol as needed is reserved for performance-only presentations.

guides.title: Week 41 · 4 Generalized Anxiety Disorder
guides.html:
SLM03 · Anxiety

Generalized Anxiety Disorder

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Uncontrollable worry with three of six symptoms for six months: criteria, epidemiology, the differential, CBT and MBCT, and first-line drugs, with the three anxiety modules side by side.

The case: Peter, 40, anxious about everything

A 40-year-old entrepreneur who lives in Toronto with his wife and three children has just opened a bakery; his wife supports the family financially and accompanies him. He feels anxious "all the time" and about "everything" — finances, his children's futures, his own success — and cannot control the worries. His concentration suffers and his mind goes blank when he tries to work; he has restless sleep, trouble falling asleep and night waking; his wife describes him as on edge and easily irritated. History: two depressive episodes in his mid-twenties treated with sertraline; atrial fibrillation on a beta blocker; a rash to paroxetine; four cups of caffeine a day; a mother and maternal aunt with "anxiety"; separation difficulty when first starting school that resolved; a supportive marriage.

On examination he is alert and cooperative with adequate hygiene, jittery and constantly playing with his watch, speech faster in rate but normal in volume and rhythm, mood "anxious", affect anxious and irritable, no perceptual disturbance, thought process over-inclusive and detail-oriented, thought content reassurance-seeking and focused on insecurities about the future, insight and judgement adequate, cognition grossly normal. The negatives do the ruling out: no perceptual disturbance excludes psychosis, normal volume and rhythm argue against mania, intact cognition excludes delirium.

Module quiz: how would you diagnose Peter?
Options were panic disorder, OCD, generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. The module's feedback gives all four exclusions: not panic disorder, because there are no recurrent unexpected panic attacks and the worry is generalized across situations; not OCD, because there are no recurrent obsessions or compulsions; not MDD, because there is no recurrent low mood; not OCPD, which is a pervasive early-adulthood personality pattern of orderliness, perfectionism and control.

Every history line is load-bearing. The paroxetine rash removes one of the three first-line SSRIs; sertraline has already worked for him. The caffeine sets up the module's advice slide and the substance-induced line of the differential. The childhood separation difficulty is resolved in the same sentence, so it is history rather than a current diagnosis.

Diagnostic criteria

The module states the criteria as three statements and a six-item menu.

  1. Excessive anxiety and worry (apprehensive expectation), occurring more days than not for at least six months, about a number of events or activities such as work or school performance.
  2. The individual finds it difficult to control the worry.
  3. The anxiety and worry are associated with three or more of six symptoms, with at least some present more days than not for the past six months:
SymptomPeter
Restlessness, feeling keyed up or on edgeWife describes him as on edge
Being easily fatiguedNot documented
Difficulty concentrating or mind going blankBoth described
IrritabilityEasily irritated
Muscle tensionNot documented
Sleep disturbance (falling or staying asleep, or restless unsatisfying sleep)All three described

Peter shows four of six against a threshold of three. Uncontrollability of the worry is a separate requirement, not part of the count. The module does not print the remaining DSM-5 criteria on distress or impairment, substances, and other disorders; their content is carried by the differential.

GAD is the only anxiety disorder in this week's modules with a symptom count. Specific phobia (criteria A–G) and social anxiety disorder (A–J) require every criterion. A stem offering "three of six" is describing GAD; all three share the six-month duration.

Epidemiology

  • Lifetime prevalence 9% in the general population; the module's own quiz keys 9% against 1%, 3%, 10% and 20%, and its point is that GAD is common.
  • Median age of onset 30; prevalence peaks in middle age and declines in later life; GAD is very unlikely to begin before adolescence, which makes it the latest-onset anxiety disorder. Social anxiety disorder, by contrast, has a median onset of 13.
  • Females are twice as likely to have GAD, a 2:1 ratio; this is the only explicit sex ratio in the three anxiety modules.
  • Reported more frequently by people of European descent and in developed countries.
  • Highly comorbid with other anxiety disorders, with major depressive disorder in up to 50%, and with substance use disorders.

Differential diagnosis

Six items, leading with organic causes: anxiety disorder due to another medical condition (the module names pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism); substance- or medication-induced anxiety disorder, for which caffeine is the module's worked example; social anxiety disorder; obsessive-compulsive disorder; PTSD and adjustment disorders; and depressive, bipolar and psychotic disorders. Panic disorder is handled by the diagnosis quiz rather than the differential slide.

GAD versusThe discriminator
Social anxiety disorderWorry confined to social or performance situations, versus spread across many activities and uncontrollable
Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected attacks, versus generalized worry without discrete uncued attacks
OCDRecurrent obsessions or compulsions, versus worry about real-life concerns
Major depressive disorderRecurrent low mood, versus anxious mood; the two coexist in up to half of GAD
OCPDA pervasive personality pattern of orderliness, perfectionism and control from early adulthood, versus episodic uncontrollable worry
Organic causesHyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, and substances such as caffeine

Psychological treatment

Seven modalities, in the module's order: psychoeducation, with the stated purpose of preventing avoidance of anxiety triggers; cognitive behavioural therapy, restructuring cognitive distortions and designing behavioural experiments to challenge them; mindfulness-based cognitive therapy; exposure therapy, extinguishing fear through repeated exposure; relaxation therapy; biofeedback; and imagery. Biofeedback and imagery appear only in this module.

The module's own quiz asks which two therapies to recommend most for Peter and keys CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. Exposure and relaxation therapy are still on the treatment list, just not the top two; psychodynamic psychotherapy, the fifth option, appears nowhere on the list and is the clear distractor.

Additional advice: caffeine and sugar

Decrease caffeinated and high-sugar drinks and foods, which can worsen anxiety. The module's infographic sets a moderate intake of 200–300 mg per day and gives serving contents:

DrinkCaffeineServing
Brewed coffee135 mg8 oz (240 mL)
Starbucks espresso70 mg1 oz (30 mL)
Monster Energy160 mg (highest)16 oz (480 mL)
Red Bull80 mg8.3 oz (250 mL)
Mountain Dew90 mg20 oz (592 mL)
Coke60 mg (lowest)20 oz (592 mL)

Peter's four cups of brewed coffee come to roughly 540 mg a day, about double the moderate ceiling — the arithmetic the slide exists to set up.

Pharmacological treatment

Pharmacological and psychological treatments have equivalent efficacy in GAD. This is the one anxiety disorder of the three where the module puts medication level with therapy; in specific phobia there is no drug, and in social anxiety disorder CBT is the gold-standard non-pharmacological treatment beside a drug list.

ClassAgents namedAlso first line in social anxiety disorder?
SSRIsEscitalopram, paroxetine, sertralineYes (that list adds fluvoxamine)
SNRIsVenlafaxine, duloxetineVenlafaxine XR yes; duloxetine is GAD-only
OtherPregabalinYes

Everything on the slide is first line; no second-line agent is named. The module's quiz on which class has the most evidence keys antidepressant over benzodiazepine, NMDA modulator and antipsychotic — the benzodiazepine is the trap, because fastest relief is not the same as best evidence. The SSRI side effects the module lists are GI symptoms, headaches, weight gain and sexual dysfunction, keyed "all of the above". Applied to Peter, the paroxetine rash rules that agent out and his prior response to sertraline makes it the natural choice.

The three anxiety disorders side by side

Specific phobiaSocial anxiety disorderGAD
Core fearA specific object or situationNegative evaluation by othersUncontrollable worry about many activities
StructureA–G, all requiredA–J, all requiredWorry + uncontrollability + 3 of 6 symptoms
Duration6 months6 monthsMore days than not for 6 months
SpecifierStimulus type (5)Performance onlyNone
FrequencyMost common disorder in women; 2nd in men2nd most common anxiety disorder9% lifetime
OnsetNot givenMedian 13; 75% at 7–15Median 30; rarely before adolescence
SexNot givenMore common in femalesFemales 2:1
TherapyCBT, gold standard; graded exposureCBT, gold-standard non-pharmacologicalCBT + MBCT; equivalent to medication
DrugsNone supportedSSRIs, venlafaxine XR, pregabalin; propranolol PRN for performance onlySSRIs, venlafaxine, duloxetine, pregabalin

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Three of six with uncontrollable worry for six months is the whole diagnosis; the six are restlessness, fatigue, concentration or mind blank, irritability, muscle tension, sleep.
  • 9%, 30, 2:1, up to 50%: prevalence, median onset, sex ratio, comorbid depression.
  • Latest onset of the anxiety disorders; a childhood-onset story points elsewhere.
  • Hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma are the named organic mimics; caffeine the named substance.
  • Antidepressant, not benzodiazepine, has the most evidence; duloxetine is first line here and not in social anxiety disorder.
  • Psychodynamic therapy is not on the list. Exposure and relaxation are on it but are not the top two.
Worry versus obsession, and worry versus personality. Worry about real-life concerns is GAD; recurrent intrusive obsessions with compulsions are OCD; a lifelong pattern of perfectionism and control is OCPD. All three can look like a preoccupied, detail-oriented patient in the room, and the module's diagnosis quiz is built on that resemblance.
GAD is excessive, uncontrollable worry about many things, more days than not for six months, with at least three of six associated symptoms. It is common (9%), begins late (median 30), affects women twice as often, and coexists with depression in up to half. Treatment is CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, or an antidepressant with equivalent efficacy: escitalopram, paroxetine or sertraline, venlafaxine or duloxetine, or pregabalin.

guides.title: Week 41 · 5 Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder & Related Disorders
guides.html:
SLM04 · OCD

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder & Related Disorders

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Obsessions, compulsions and the related-disorder family; the differential; SSRIs started low and pushed high; and exposure with response prevention.

The case: Jane, 35, germs and rituals

A 35-year-old teacher living with her husband and one-year-old son has had increasing concerns about germs and getting people sick since giving birth. Over a year she has spent more and more time in elaborate handwashing, disinfecting and cleaning rituals: she has been late for work several times because of cleaning at home, spends over 90 minutes in the shower after work, and her hands are red, raw and cracked from washing and sanitizer. She had some checking behaviours in childhood that resolved without treatment; no medications; a glass of wine with dinner once or twice a week; a sister with depression and a mother with GAD; a father who recently died of complications of an infection; good supports.

The case maps onto the criteria directly: the obsession is contamination and harm to others, the compulsions are washing, disinfecting and cleaning performed to reduce that discomfort, and the severity criterion is met on all three limbs — marked distress, more than an hour a day (the shower alone), and interference with work. The father's death from an infection and the postpartum period are the psychosocial context; the childhood checking is the module's nod to an early, waxing-and-waning course.

The obsessive-compulsive and related disorders

The DSM-5 chapter lists obsessive-compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder), excoriation (skin-picking) disorder, substance- or medication-induced and medical-condition-related forms, and other specified and unspecified categories. The module focuses on OCD and defines the related disorders through the differential.

Related disorderCore featureDiscriminator from OCD
Body dysmorphic disorderObsessions and compulsions about physical appearanceContent limited to appearance
Hoarding disorderPersistent difficulty discarding possessions, marked distress on discarding, excessive accumulationSymptoms exclusively about discarding and accumulation. If hoarding is driven by typical OCD obsessions such as incompleteness or harm prevention, the diagnosis is OCD instead
TrichotillomaniaCompulsive hair pullingLimited to hair pulling, in the absence of obsessions
Excoriation disorderNamed in the family list onlyBy analogy, a body-focused repetitive behaviour of skin picking without obsessions; the module gives no criteria

DSM-5 criteria for OCD

A. Obsessions, compulsions, or both.

ObsessionsCompulsions
Persistent unwanted thoughts, images or impulsesRepetitive behaviours or mental acts
Intrusive, uncontrollable or excessivePerformed in response to an obsession, or in ritualistic fashion
Provoke anxietyIntended to reduce discomfort or prevent a feared event
Attempts to ignore, suppress or neutralize them with another thought or action

B. Severity — the symptoms cause marked distress, occupy more than one hour a day, or significantly interfere with functioning. C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. D. Not better explained by another mental disorder.

Specifiers: insight is graded as good or fair, poor, or absent with delusional beliefs; and tic-related applies with a current or past tic disorder. Two wording points matter: obsessions alone, compulsions alone, or both satisfy criterion A; and compulsions include mental acts, which is why mental review counts as a ritual.

Epidemiology and course

  • Lifetime prevalence 2–3%.
  • Severe: the WHO's tenth leading cause of disability.
  • Mean age of onset 19.5, with an earlier peak in males; earlier than PTSD's mid-to-late twenties.
  • High comorbidity with depression and anxiety disorders; a chronic course.
  • Familial: about 10% of first-degree relatives are affected, three to five times the population rate.

Obsessions and their rituals

The module's matching exercise pairs four obsession types with their rituals:

Obsessive thoughtCorresponding rituals
ContaminationWashing, checking
DoubtingChecking, reassurance seeking, mental review or rituals
Aggressive or sexual thoughts, images or impulsesChecking, reassurance seeking, mental review or rituals
Symmetry or exactnessOrdering, arranging, placing objects "just so"

Doubting and aggressive or sexual intrusions share a ritual set; what separates them is the content of the obsession. Contamination's rituals include checking as well as washing. Jane is the contamination row.

Differential diagnosis

ConditionThe discriminator
GADWorries are about real-life concerns; OCD obsessions usually are not and can be odd, irrational or magical, with linked compulsions
Specific phobiaThe feared object is much more circumscribed and rituals are absent
Social anxiety disorderFear limited to social interactions
Major depressive disorderRumination is mood-congruent, not necessarily intrusive, and not linked to compulsions
Anorexia nervosaIn OCD the obsessions and compulsions are not limited to weight and food
Tics and stereotyped movementsLess complex, not aimed at neutralizing obsessions; tics follow premonitory sensory urges, compulsions follow obsessions. Both diagnoses may be given
Psychotic disordersEven with absent insight, OCD patients have obsessions and compulsions and no hallucinations or formal thought disorder
Paraphilias, gambling, substance useThe person derives pleasure from the activity and resists it only because of its consequences
OCPDNo intrusions and no response-driven rituals; an enduring pattern of perfectionism and rigid control. Both diagnoses can be given

A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic motor movement or vocalization (eye blinking, throat clearing); a stereotyped movement is a repetitive, seemingly driven, non-functional motor behaviour (head banging, body rocking, self-biting).

Treatment

The algorithm

After assessment, therapy and medication are parallel options joined by "and/or", not steps in sequence; the only first-line drug class is the SSRI. Two notes govern the choice: CBT is equivalent or superior to pharmacotherapy, and the combination is superior to medication alone but not to CBT alone. The module gives no augmentation or treatment-resistance pathway.

Drugs

LineAgents
First line: SSRIsEscitalopram, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine
Second lineClomipramine (a tricyclic) and venlafaxine XR (an SNRI)

All five first-line agents are SSRIs. Clomipramine is the only tricyclic named in the module, and it is second line. Venlafaxine XR is second line here but first line for PTSD.

Principles of pharmacotherapy

  1. The treatment goal is improvement, not remission.
  2. Start low and aim high.
  3. Be patient: response often takes 6–12 weeks.
  4. An adequate trial requires 12–15 weeks.
  5. Treatment is long term: at least one year.
  6. Discontinue very slowly.
  7. High relapse rates unless combined with behavioural strategies.
Two windows, easily swapped. Response is expected at 6–12 weeks; an adequate trial is 12–15 weeks; and CBT runs 12–15 weekly one-hour sessions. The drug trial and the therapy course share a number and are different things.

CBT and exposure with response prevention

CBT for OCD is highly structured over 12–15 weekly one-hour sessions and has six components: education, exposure and response prevention, cognitive interventions, family involvement where appropriate, problem-solving skills, and relapse prevention. ERP is one component of CBT, not a synonym for it. Its four steps:

  1. Define a range of obsessional triggers.
  2. Rank the degree of discomfort with each, on a 10-point scale or out of 100%.
  3. Build a hierarchy, most distressing at the top.
  4. Expose the patient systematically to each trigger while preventing rituals and avoidance.
Contamination hierarchyDistress (0–100)
Touching a public toilet seat80
Touching the toilet seat at home70
Touching a public washroom door handle65
Picking something up from the floor and handing it to someone, "spreading" contamination65
Eating something that fell on the floor60
Touching elevator buttons50
Touching the floor40
Petting pets30
Sorting dirty laundry25

The scale's anchors are 100 highest, 75 significant, 50 moderate, 25 mild, 0 none. The steps are small (no gap over 10), ties are allowed, the same act differs by context (public versus home toilet), and exposure starts at the bottom.

Why exposure works

After a trigger, anxiety rises steeply with an urge to ritualize. If the compulsion is performed, anxiety drops abruptly back to baseline, which is highly reinforcing; anxiety returns with the next trigger, the peaks stay the same height, and more and more time goes into rituals. With repeated exposure and response prevention, the patient learns that the feared consequences do not occur and that anxiety is time-limited and comes down on its own: each successive peak is lower and shorter, settling onto the same low plateau — habituation.

Compulsion cycleExposure and habituation
What ends the risePerforming the compulsionWaiting it out with response prevention
Shape of the declineAbrupt drop to baselineGradual descent, sooner each time
Peak height over repetitionsConstantProgressively lower
Effect on the disorderShort-term relief; more ritualizingLong-term reduction; feared outcomes disconfirmed

Medication or CBT

MedicationCBT
ProsEasy to take; safe; helps OCD symptoms; effective for common comorbidities; readily availableVery effective; safe; longer-lasting effects than medication alone
ConsLimited benefit in many patients; side effects; higher relapse than CBTRequires motivation and hard work; can be difficult to access

Discriminators and exam traps

  • More than one hour a day is the severity number; 2–3% the prevalence; 19.5 the mean onset; 10% in first-degree relatives.
  • Worry about real problems is GAD; odd or magical intrusions with rituals are OCD; lifelong perfectionism without intrusions is OCPD.
  • Hoarding driven by incompleteness or harm obsessions is OCD, not hoarding disorder.
  • Pleasure marks the pseudo-compulsions: gambling, paraphilias and substance use are enjoyed; OCD rituals are not.
  • Combination beats medication alone, not CBT alone.
  • Clomipramine and venlafaxine XR are second line; all five first-line agents are SSRIs.
  • Tics follow premonitory urges; compulsions follow obsessions.
OCD is intrusive obsessions and neutralizing compulsions that cost more than an hour a day or cause marked distress or impairment, with insight graded and a tic-related specifier. It is common, early-onset, familial and chronic. Treatment is CBT with exposure and response prevention, an SSRI started low and pushed high over a 12-to-15-week trial and continued at least a year, or both; the combination beats medication alone but not CBT alone.

guides.title: Week 41 · 6 Post-traumatic Stress Disorder & Acute Stress Disorder
guides.html:
SLM05 · Trauma

Post-traumatic Stress Disorder & Acute Stress Disorder

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The four symptom clusters at 1/1/2/2, the one-month line that separates PTSD from acute stress disorder, epidemiology, and trauma-focused CBT with an antidepressant.

The case: Annie, 30, three months after an assault

A 30-year-old criminal lawyer living in Toronto with her husband and three-year-old son has a three-month history of persistent low mood and recurrent memories and flashbacks of being cornered and strangled by a client while visiting him in prison. Since then she becomes distressed when alone with a man in a room, has refused cases where the client is still in jail, is constantly scanning her surroundings for threats, and has halved her workload because she cannot concentrate. No psychiatric history; polycystic ovarian syndrome on metformin and an oral contraceptive; a 2.5 pack-year smoking history; a mother and sister with depression; a stable upbringing, good relationships, and a good marriage in which she nonetheless cannot confide her symptoms.

On examination she is alert and cooperative, startled by loud noises with increased psychomotor activity, speech normal, mood "I can't feel good", affect dysphoric and anxious, no perceptual disturbance, thought process linear, thought content her memories and worry about whether she will improve, insight, judgement and cognition intact.

ClusterAnnie's evidence
ExposureDirectly experienced threatened death: strangled by a client
Intrusion (needs 1)Recurrent memories; flashbacks
Avoidance (needs 1)Refuses cases with jailed clients; distress alone with a man is the cue
Negative cognition and mood (needs 2)Persistent low mood; cannot feel good; detachment from her husband
Arousal and reactivity (needs 2)Hypervigilance; exaggerated startle; poor concentration
DurationThree months: past the one-month line, so PTSD rather than acute stress disorder
ImpairmentWorkload cut in half

The module's diagnosis quiz keys PTSD over major depressive episode, OCD, GAD and social anxiety disorder. Depression does not account for flashbacks, hypervigilance and trauma-specific avoidance; OCD needs obsessions and compulsions, and her intrusions are trauma memories; GAD worries are about real-life concerns rather than one event; social anxiety is fear of social interaction, whereas her fear is specifically of being alone with a man after a strangulation by one. Her family history of depression is what makes the depressive episode a live distractor, and her clean MSE rules out the psychotic differential.

Diagnostic criteria

Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence by any of four routes: directly; witnessing; learning that a traumatic event happened to a loved one; or repeated exposure through occupation. Indirect exposure counts. Then four symptom clusters:

ClusterItemsNeeds
IntrusionRecurrent involuntary intrusive memories · recurrent distressing dreams · dissociative reactions (flashbacks) · psychological distress with reminders · physiological reaction to reminders1 of 5
AvoidanceAvoidance of associated memories, thoughts or feelings · avoidance of external reminders (people, places)1 of 2
Negative cognition and moodInability to remember an important aspect of the event · persistent exaggerated negative beliefs about self, others or the world · distorted cognitions about cause or consequences leading to blame · persistent negative emotional state · diminished interest or participation · detachment or estrangement · inability to have positive emotions2 of 7
Arousal and reactivityIrritability and angry outbursts · reckless or self-destructive behaviour · hypervigilance · exaggerated startle · concentration difficulties · sleep disturbance2 of 6

Plus duration over one month, significant distress or impairment, and not due to a substance or another medical condition.

The pattern is 1 / 1 / 2 / 2: one intrusion, one avoidance, two negative cognition or mood, two arousal. Menu length does not track the threshold — intrusion has five items and needs only one; avoidance has two and needs one; the two clusters needing two are the long ones (seven and six).

The module lists no specifiers. In DSM-5 there are two, outside this module's content: a dissociative subtype (depersonalization or derealization) and delayed expression (full criteria not met until at least six months after the event).

Epidemiology and risk

  • Lifetime prevalence 9%; the module's quiz keys the band 6–9%. On a multiple-choice paper the band is the answer; as a figure, 9%. The 1–3% distractor is OCD's number.
  • Twice as common in females.
  • Onset varies, typically in the mid-to-late twenties; the quiz keys 25–30. OCD begins earlier, at a mean of 19.5.
  • Higher rates in Aboriginal peoples, refugees and African-Americans, stated twice in the module.
  • The most common source of trauma is sexual or relationship violence; the other trauma types on the quiz are organized violence (kidnapping, war), interpersonal violence (assault) and interpersonal-network trauma (death or life-threatening illness of a loved one).
  • Comorbid with substance use, major depression and anxiety; physical comorbidities include angina, heart failure, bronchitis, asthma, peripheral artery disease and liver disease; high functional impairment; suicide risk increased two- to three-fold.

Risk factors: temperament as a child, childhood adversity, family dysfunction, family psychiatric history, lower socioeconomic status, lower education, and younger age at the time of trauma. Annie has almost none of these apart from a family history of depression, which is the module's point: PTSD occurs without a loaded risk profile.

Acute stress disorder, PTSD and adjustment disorder

The psychiatric differential lists acute stress disorder, adjustment disorder, GAD, OCD, major depressive episode, personality disorder, dissociative disorder, conversion disorder and psychotic disorder; the medical differential is traumatic brain injury if physical trauma occurred and neurological damage, since a trauma severe enough to cause PTSD may also have injured the head. The module works through only one of these.

Acute stress disorderPTSDAdjustment disorder
TimingSymptoms in the first 30 days after the eventDisturbance lasting over one monthOnset within three months of the stressor
StressorA highly traumatic eventActual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violenceAny identifiable stressor, which need not reach the trauma threshold
PicturePTSD symptoms with functional impairmentThe four clusters at 1/1/2/2Symptoms out of proportion to the stressor, not meeting criteria for another disorder
CourseMost recover; a subset persists past 30 days and becomes PTSDChronic risk, comorbidity, raised suicide riskResolves as the stressor resolves

The module defines only the first two columns; its stated rule is that time of onset distinguishes PTSD from acute stress disorder. Adjustment disorder is named on the differential but never defined there; the third column is standard DSM-5 teaching.

Treatment

Psychotherapy

ModalityWhat it is
Trauma-focused CBTPsychoeducation, relaxation, affect regulation, cognitive processing of the trauma, a trauma narrative, mastery of trauma reminders. The most effective modality and the mainstay.
EMDREye movement desensitization and reprocessing: rhythmic movements or sounds during processing of trauma memories
Cognitive processing therapyCognitive therapy plus written accounts of the trauma (printed on one slide as "cognitive reprocessing therapy")
Prolonged exposureGradual confrontation of trauma-related memories, feelings and situations
Stress inoculationCoping skills for PTSD symptoms
DBTAimed at reducing self-harm in borderline personality disorder; listed, not a PTSD treatment as such

The module keys two different answers on purpose. Asked which therapy is most effective, the key is trauma-focused CBT. Asked what to recommend most for Annie from a list that does not include trauma-focused CBT (mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, EMDR, psychodynamic psychotherapy, interpersonal therapy, relaxation therapy), the key is EMDR, the only trauma-processing therapy offered.

Pharmacotherapy

First line is an antidepressant: the SSRIs fluoxetine, paroxetine and sertraline, and the SNRI venlafaxine XR. The module's treatment-choice quiz keys antidepressant over benzodiazepine, ECT and antipsychotic. No dose, trial length or second line is given. Two cross-module points: the PTSD SSRI list is shorter than OCD's, with no escitalopram or fluvoxamine; and venlafaxine XR is first line in PTSD but second line in OCD.

Benzodiazepines are not the treatment for PTSD. The module never prints a prohibition, but it keys the benzodiazepine wrong against the antidepressant, and the Canadian guideline it cites recommends against them. A stem offering a benzodiazepine for PTSD symptoms is a distractor.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • 1/1/2/2 and over one month. Under one month with the same picture is acute stress disorder, and most such patients recover.
  • Learning of a loved one's trauma and occupational exposure count as criterion-A exposure.
  • 6–9% (or 9%), twice as common in women, onset in the mid-to-late twenties, suicide risk two to three times.
  • Sexual or relationship violence is the most common trauma source.
  • Trauma-focused CBT is most effective; EMDR is the answer when TF-CBT is not offered; DBT is the distractor.
  • Fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine XR; not a benzodiazepine.
  • A head injury can coexist: traumatic brain injury is the medical differential.
PTSD follows exposure to death, serious injury or sexual violence, directly or indirectly, with at least one intrusion, one avoidance, two negative cognition or mood, and two arousal symptoms lasting over a month with impairment. It affects about 9% of people, women twice as often, and raises suicide risk two- to three-fold. Trauma-focused CBT and an antidepressant (an SSRI or venlafaxine XR) are the mainstays; time separates it from acute stress disorder.

guides.title: Week 41 · 7 Suicide Risk Assessment
guides.html:
SLM06 · Risk

Suicide Risk Assessment

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Epidemiology, the bio-psycho-social risk factors and SAD PERSONS, how to ask, and the four-step assessment from plan and intent to protective factors.

Why it matters

  • Suicide is common. In 2013 there were over 4,000 suicides in Canada; suicide was the ninth leading cause of death overall and the second leading cause of death at ages 15 to 24.
  • Risk is highest in mid-life: people aged 40 to 59 have the highest suicide rates.
  • The gender paradox: females are three to four times more likely to attempt suicide; males are more likely to die by it.
Two age facts, easily conflated. The highest rate is at ages 40 to 59. The ranking as second leading cause of death is at ages 15 to 24, because young people die of little else. Both are the module's own statements; a question will ask for one or the other.

The module has a single objective: recognize and list the risk factors for suicide in depressive disorders. It is an interviewing and assessment module. It contains no safety-planning protocol, no means-restriction counselling, no admission or certification criteria and no follow-up plan; the only therapeutic instruction is to validate suffering and instill hope.

Risk factors: biological, psychological, social

BiologicalPsychologicalSocial
AgeHistory of suicide attempt(s)Marital status (single more than married)
Male sexHopelessnessNo children
Medical illnessDecreased self-esteemLack of supports
PainImpulsivityUnemployed
History of mental illnessPsychomotor agitation or restlessnessStressful life events
Substance useAccess to lethal means
Family history of suicide

Eighteen factors: seven biological, five psychological, six social. The placements that get tested are the counter-intuitive ones: a history of attempts is psychological, family history of suicide is biological, access to lethal means is social, and psychomotor agitation is the one item that is an examination finding rather than a history point.

The mnemonic: SAD PERSONS

LetterItem
SSex (male more than female)
AAge (under 20 or over 45)
DDepression
PPrevious attempt(s)
EEthanol or other substance use
RRational thinking loss (psychosis)
SSocial supports lacking
OOrganized plan
NNo spouse
SSickness or pain

The module uses SAD PERSONS as a checklist, not a scored scale: no points, no cut-offs, no disposition rules. The age cut-offs of under 20 or over 45 come from the 1983 scale and sit beside the module's separate statement that rates peak at 40 to 59; a question quoting the mnemonic wants the cut-offs. When the module applies the mnemonic to its video patient, the seventh item is printed as "suicide in family" and the ninth as "no spouse (lack of supports)"; the standard version above is the one to learn.

The strongest predictor the module names
"A history of previous attempts is one of the most powerful predictors of suicide for all age groups. Always ask about a history of prior suicide attempts." If a question asks for the single strongest risk factor in the module, this is it.

Asking about suicide

The module's quiz states the myth and rejects it: asking about suicide does not make patients more likely to think about it or raise their risk. The two points that follow are that bringing up the topic does not increase risk, and that the real obstacle is the clinician's own discomfort. Patients will not necessarily volunteer suicidal thoughts, so the clinician asks, frankly and calmly, using empathic or normalizing statements. Two model openings:

  • "Sometimes people with depression feel so terrible they wonder if life is worth living. Have you had thoughts of ending your life?"
  • "It sounds like you have been under a terrible amount of stress. Have you had any thoughts that life isn't worth living?"

Both normalize first and then ask directly. An oblique question ("you're not thinking of doing anything silly, are you?") is the wrong answer on a station.

The four-step assessment

1. Current plan and intent

Once any suicidal thinking is acknowledged, probe: "What kinds of thoughts have you had about ending your life?" Then separate three things in order.

  • Ideation, passive or active. Passive: a wish to be dead or never to wake up. Active: a specific plan such as jumping from a height, hanging, or overdosing.
  • Plan, and whether it is feasible with available means. "Which pills would you take?" "Do you have access to these pills?"
  • Intent, and whether they have started to act. "You've had thoughts of taking an overdose. Do you think this is something you might actually do?"

2. Intensity of the thinking

How often; whether more frequent; how intense, and whether they can resist; whether they have acted; practised or aborted attempts ("Have you held the pills in your hand and thought about taking them? What happened?"); arrangements such as a suicide note or a will; a chosen time or place. The slide's closing instruction is be specific. Rehearsal and preparation are the highest-yield items here.

3. Risk factors

Run the SAD PERSONS list against the patient, and always ask about prior attempts.

4. Protective factors

Ask about hope and elicit ambivalence about dying. Three model questions: "Do you have some hope that things can get better?"; "I wonder if there's a part of you that wants to live?"; "What has stopped you from acting on these thoughts?" The protective factors: children, spouse or other family; pets; religious beliefs; intact self-esteem or the ability to identify strengths; and a strong therapeutic alliance, the one factor the clinician creates in the interview itself, which is why this step comes last.

Putting it together

  1. Suicide is common.
  2. Do not assume patients will disclose suicidal thoughts; ask whenever it might be occurring.
  3. Gather details of plans and intent. Be specific.
  4. Identify risk factors.
  5. Elicit protective factors that might contribute to ambivalence.
  6. Validate suffering and instill hope.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Rate peaks at 40 to 59; second leading cause of death at 15 to 24; ninth overall; over 4,000 a year.
  • Women attempt three to four times more often; men die more often.
  • Previous attempts is the strongest predictor and is filed under psychological factors.
  • Asking does not increase risk. The barrier is the clinician's discomfort.
  • Ideation, then plan and means, then intent; feasibility and access are the questions most often dropped.
  • Practised or aborted attempts and arrangements mark rehearsal.
  • Protective factors are elicited by asking about hope and ambivalence, and the alliance itself is one of them.
Suicide is common, peaks in mid-life, and is attempted more by women and completed more by men. Assessment runs plan and intent, intensity, SAD PERSONS risk factors with previous attempts as the strongest, and protective factors elicited through hope and ambivalence, asked frankly and specifically, because asking does not create risk and patients rarely volunteer it.

guides.title: Week 41 · 8 Mental Disorders due to Another Medical Condition

SLM07 · Differential

Mental Disorders due to Another Medical Condition

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

When a medical condition causes the psychiatric picture: criteria A–E, the disorder-specific criterion A, the competing explanations, and the conditions that induce mood or anxiety symptoms.

The concept

Some medical conditions produce psychiatric symptoms as a direct pathophysiological consequence of the condition, and the psychiatric symptoms improve when the underlying condition is treated, if it is treatable. This excludes psychosocial reactions to having an illness. Those two halves are the whole diagnosis: causation through pathophysiology, with symptoms tracking the medical condition, and explicit exclusion of the psychological reaction to being ill, which is an adjustment disorder or a primary mood or anxiety disorder instead.

The DSM-5 family named in the module: bipolar and related disorder, depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, psychotic disorder, obsessive-compulsive and related disorder, and personality change, each "due to another medical condition", with the list marked as non-exhaustive.

DSM-5 criteria

Criterion
AThe disorder represents a clinically significant symptomatic presentation of a relevant mental disorder
BThere is evidence from the history, physical examination or laboratory findings that the disturbance is the direct pathophysiological consequence of another medical condition
CNot better explained by another mental disorder
DDoes not occur exclusively during a delirium
ECauses clinically significant distress or impairment, or necessitates hospitalization to prevent harm to self or others, or there are psychotic features
Criterion A is the only disorder-specific criterion; B through E are identical for every "due to another medical condition" diagnosis. Criterion E is satisfied by any one of three things: distress or impairment, hospitalization to prevent harm, or psychotic features.

The disorder-specific criterion A

DisorderCriterion A
Depressive disorder due to AMCA prominent and persistent period of depressed mood or markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all or almost all activities that predominates in the clinical picture
Bipolar and related disorder due to AMCA prominent and persistent period of abnormally elevated, expansive or irritable mood and abnormally increased activity or energy that predominates in the clinical picture
Anxiety disorder due to AMCPanic attacks or anxiety is predominant in the clinical picture

All three turn on the symptom predominating in the clinical picture. The depressive variant uses the two MDD gate symptoms with no five-of-nine count and no two-week duration; the bipolar variant uses the DSM-5 two-part mania gate, mood and energy; the anxiety variant is the loosest. None carries a duration threshold or symptom count: the diagnosis rests on predominance plus the causal evidence of criterion B.

What counts as a direct consequence: the module's quiz

ScenarioDirect consequence?The module's reason
Anxiety in large open spaces from fear of not finding a bathroom, in symptomatic Crohn's diseaseNoA psychological reaction to having a symptom; the anxiety is not a direct result of the inflammatory process
Low energy, motivation and mood with onset two days after a middle cerebral artery strokeYesPost-stroke depression, independent of the psychological effects of acquired disability, is a commonly seen phenomenon
Recurrent untriggered panic attacks that remit after surgical excision of a pheochromocytomaYesThe panic symptoms represent a pathophysiological consequence of excess catecholamine
Low mood and hopelessness with onset four weeks after a diagnosis of testicular cancerNoThe cancer was present for some time before the diagnosis; the symptoms represent a psychological reaction to being diagnosed

The testicular-cancer item is the instructive trap: the symptoms track the news, not the pathophysiology, since the tumour predated the mood change. The stroke item tracks the event by two days; the pheochromocytoma item is keyed on remission after treatment, the module's own rule.

Reality is multifactorial

The module raises its own objection: how does one know the stroke caused the depression, rather than the stress of a major illness or the loss of function? Its answer is a four-way differential of competing explanations, each excluded by a criterion.

Competing explanationWhat the module saysCriterion that excludes it
Pre-morbid or co-morbid psychiatric conditionAn existing mood or anxiety disorder may predate the medical condition and may worsen through pathophysiology or through the new stressorC
Psychological distress or adjustment disorderA psychological reaction to the diagnosis or progression of illnessB fails: no direct pathophysiological consequence
DeliriumRapid-onset, fluctuating changes in attention and orientation in the acutely ill; symptoms occurring only during delirium are not a disorder due to AMCD
Medication-induced disorderTreatments such as prednisone and anti-retrovirals can induce psychiatric symptomsB: the cause is the drug, so the label is medication-induced

The HIV worked example

Depressive symptoms in a person with HIV/AIDS can arise by three biological pathways, each with its own label, alongside a psychosocial stream:

PathwayDiagnosis
Effect of the HIV virus on the CNSDepressive disorder due to another medical condition
Effect of antiretroviral medications on the CNSMedication-induced depressive disorder
High prevalence of comorbid drug useSubstance-induced depressive disorder
Societal and self-stigma; illness perceived as chronic and incurablePsychosocial: increases risk of mood problems, but produces neither "due to" label

One patient, one symptom picture, three distinct labels depending on the pathway. Depressed mood in a person with HIV who has just started an antiretroviral is a medication-induced question, not a "due to another medical condition" one.

Making the diagnosis: three factors

  1. Time course. The psychiatric symptoms clearly onset, exacerbate or remit with changes in the status of the medical condition. The stroke item is the onset limb; the pheochromocytoma item is the remit limb.
  2. Atypical features. Features less associated with a primary disorder, such as rapid onset, or age or gender outside the typical risk period; the module's example is onset of panic disorder symptoms at age 70.
  3. Pathophysiological mechanism. The medical disorder has a known or plausible mechanism for producing the symptoms; the bar is plausibility, not proof.

Conditions that induce mood or anxiety symptoms

Depressive symptomsManic symptomsAnxiety symptoms
StrokeStrokeHyperthyroidism
Traumatic brain injuryTraumatic brain injuryPheochromocytoma
Parkinson's diseaseCushing's diseasePorphyria
Cushing's diseaseMultiple sclerosisCNS neoplasms
HIV infectionHIV infection
CNS neoplasms

Four conditions appear in both the depressive and manic columns: stroke, traumatic brain injury, Cushing's disease and HIV. Parkinson's disease is unique to depressive; multiple sclerosis to manic. The anxiety column is entirely endocrine, metabolic and neoplastic and shares nothing with the depressive column; hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma are the two classic panic mimics, and pheochromocytoma is the one the quiz uses. CNS neoplasms are printed in the manic and anxiety columns only.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Pathophysiology, not reaction. Fear of an incontinence accident in Crohn's and grief after a cancer diagnosis are reactions; post-stroke depression and pheochromocytoma panic are consequences.
  • The clock is the disease, not the diagnosis. Symptoms four weeks after a diagnosis of a tumour that has been present for months are not tracking the pathophysiology.
  • Only criterion A changes between the depressive, bipolar and anxiety forms; there are no counts or durations.
  • Only during delirium does not count; symptoms persisting outside delirious episodes are not excluded.
  • Drug versus disease: the same picture in HIV is "due to AMC" if from the virus, "medication-induced" if from the antiretroviral, "substance-induced" if from drug use.
  • Atypical onset, such as new panic at 70, is a red flag for a medical cause.
Prednisone and antiretrovirals are the module's two named culprit drugs, and Cushing's disease sits in both the depressive and manic columns. A steroid-treated patient with new mood symptoms is a medication-induced question; a patient with endogenous cortisol excess is a "due to another medical condition" question.
A disorder due to another medical condition is a predominant mood, manic or anxiety picture that is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition, evidenced by history, examination or laboratory findings, not better explained by another disorder, not confined to delirium, and impairing. Diagnose it on time course, atypical features and a plausible mechanism, and keep it apart from adjustment reactions, delirium, and medication- or substance-induced disorders.
