SLM08 · Ethics

Physicians, Human Rights & Civil Liberties: Lessons from the Holocaust

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How well-meaning physicians took part in genocide, the codes that followed, the Canadian and American parallels, and the everyday dehumanization the module asks students to recognize.

Why this is taught in medical school

The Holocaust was the largest mass killing in history, and German physicians played a significant role in supporting, rationalizing, planning and carrying out the genocide. Yet 15 to 22% of Canadians have not heard of it. The module's central claim is that Nazi doctors were not monsters who abandoned medicine: they believed they were fulfilling a "therapeutic imperative", helping society as a whole, and their racism and dehumanization of their victims let them see genocide as treatment. Asked how he reconciled his oath with killing, the Nazi doctor Fritz Klein answered that out of respect for human life he would remove a gangrenous appendix from a diseased body, and that "the Jew is the gangrenous appendix in the body of mankind". The medical metaphor did the moral work; the oath was reinterpreted rather than broken. Dismissing such people as inhuman misses the point that well-meaning humans justified and carried out these acts, which is why understanding them is the only protection against justifying unethical behaviour in ourselves.

Background

WhenWhat
1933Hitler democratically elected chancellor; Germany becomes a totalitarian dictatorship. The mechanism was legal and electoral.
1930sNewspapers, entertainment, educational materials and public discourse portray Jews as rats, subhumans, parasites and viruses, blamed for Germany's misfortunes after the First World War: "it's wrong to kill a person, but permissible to exterminate a rat"
1939Expansion into Poland starts the Second World War
1941–1945"The Final Solution": systematic murder of Jews and others deemed undesirable

Nazi antisemitism drew on over 2,000 years of scapegoating, and is distinctive in casting Jews as both "less than" and "more than": subhuman, yet rich, powerful, subversive and pulling the strings of governments and economies. Most racism dehumanizes downward; antisemitism does both at once, which is why conspiracy theory is its native form.

Eleven million civilian non-combatants were murdered, including six million Jews, 250,000 people with disabilities, 200,000 Roma, thousands of Jehovah's Witnesses, gay men, Black people and political opponents, and millions of Eastern European civilians — in industrialized extermination camps such as Auschwitz, where victims were shipped by train into gas chambers, and in mass shootings, where local populations sometimes helped identify and round up Jews.

What physicians did

  • They volunteered. A large share of Nazi academics were doctors; more than half of German doctors were early members of the Nazi party; the German Medical Association documented its members' support without coercion. "We had no choice" is false.
  • They led the escalation. Physicians sterilized hundreds of thousands of people with "hereditary diseases", progressing to systematic euthanasia of disabled children and the mentally ill, and then to industrialized genocide. Disabled and mentally ill people were the first victims, and physicians ran that phase.
  • They ran the camps' killing. Three roles: selecting who went to the gas chamber and who to the labour camp, overseeing the gas chambers, and performing experiments on non-consenting subjects.
  • The experiments: oxygen deprivation, freezing, infection with malaria or typhus, mustard gas, forced ingestion of seawater, induced gangrene in wounds, and experiments on twins including amputations, poisonings and dissections. Most served the war effort.
  • The justification was the common good: purifying and protecting the German people from a group perceived as parasitic. Utilitarian in form, built on a dehumanized premise, and dressed as public health.

Four lessons

1. Research ethics

The Nuremberg Trials of 1946 included the Doctors' Trial, in which 20 of 23 defendants were physicians, and through it the world learned of the experiments. The trials produced the Nuremberg Code, the first generally accepted code governing research on human subjects: ten conditions, of which the module names informed consent, avoiding unnecessary mental or physical harm, and the right to withdraw consent at any time. The Code heavily informed the Declaration of Helsinki, which still governs medical research today.

2. Dehumanizing discourse

The Holocaust did not happen "out of the blue"; it followed a decade of increasingly dehumanizing ways of talking about and treating Jews and other marginalized groups. Dehumanization makes it easier to treat people as undeserving of sympathy or rights, to blame them for their own or the nation's misfortune, and to treat them unfairly or cruelly. The module states that the categorization of human races as biologically distinct is not consistent with human genome mapping, and that treating race as biological rather than a social construct has itself been used to justify inequity.

Dehumanizing discourse inside medicine
Discussing patients as their problems ("the heart failure in room 32") · blaming obese patients, smokers and people who use drugs for any problem they develop · treating patients with cognitive issues as less important or less deserving of excellent care · speaking disparagingly of underhoused patients · disparaging language and poor care for racialized patients, as happened to Joyce Echaquan in Quebec. Recognizing such discourse in ourselves comes first.

3. Resisting authority

"I was just following orders" became synonymous with complicity, and since the Holocaust it is unacceptable as an excuse. Physicians may be especially vulnerable, because the profession shares two features with the regime: a culture of conformity and deference to hierarchy, and an ethical imperative to help, which in Nazi Germany became the imperative to "cleanse" society. Having a moral mission is itself a risk when the mission is redirected. Resistance existed: Oskar Schindler saved 1,200 Jews, and in Rome in 1943 doctors at Fatebenefratelli Hospital invented "Syndrome K", a fictional diagnosis created by Dr. Adriano Ossicini to mark healthy Jews who needed hiding; when Nazis inspected, the "patients" coughed to simulate tuberculosis and dozens were saved. Where Klein used a medical frame to justify killing, Ossicini used one to protect life. The module's normative conclusion: we are obligated to fight unethical practice even in the face of personal consequences.

4. Intergenerational trauma

Intergenerational trauma was first recognized in Holocaust survivors and their descendants. Children and grandchildren of genocide survivors can show complex post-traumatic stress disorder and other effects of their forebears' mistreatment. The phenomenon is now recognized in descendants of other wars and genocides, of enslaved people, and of Indigenous Peoples, including the intergenerational health effects of colonial practices and systemic racism across Turtle Island.

Atrocities by "well-meaning" physicians in North America

CaseWhat happenedThe lesson
Tuskegee syphilis study, 1932–1972The US Public Health Service recruited 600 Black men in rural Alabama to "free healthcare", told them they had "bad blood", gave placebo, and studied the natural history of untreated syphilis. Penicillin was standard by 1947 and was withheld for 25 more years; information was withheld and access to treatment elsewhere blocked. Ended by a whistleblower.Produced the 1979 Belmont Report, the American counterpart of the Nuremberg Code
Residential schools, CanadaThousands of Indigenous children died; at some schools in the early 1900s up to 70% died of tuberculosis alone. Doctors did not intervene to stop forcible removals of children with TB into those conditions. Later, nutrition experiments on hundreds of children from six schools while the remedy, ending imposed starvation, was already known.Silence is participation; the medical establishment proactively carried out a colonizing agenda: fomented smallpox epidemics, experiments in Indian Hospitals, forced sterilization, abductions
Sterilization of Indigenous womenAlberta's Sexual Sterilization Act, 1928–1972: over 2,800 women sterilized as "defective" and "unfit to produce children". From 1969 to 1972, Indigenous and Métis people were over 25% of those sterilized but 2.5% of the population. Justified as an "act of mercy".Altruism as cover for a human rights violation; the same structure as the "therapeutic imperative"
ICE detainees, September 2020Project South reported hysterectomies on detained immigrant women without full informed consent, raised by a nurse; internet translation and fellow detainees were used instead of a medical language line. The module notes the allegations are under investigation.Consent fails at the language line; this is contemporary

The two cases

Scenario 1. A second-year student in the emergency department is offered a first-ever suture on a prominent forehead laceration in a 34-year-old woman with features of Down syndrome. Introduced as "the student doctor", the student privately raises concern about the visible site; the physician replies that the patient is "slow-minded, it's not like she's going to care". The threads: dehumanizing language about a patient with a cognitive disability; a title that obscures the learner's status and undermines consent; hierarchy pressing a junior to comply. The discussion questions ask about informed consent, the effect of language on power and treatment, and how active inclusion of patients in decisions protects against dehumanization, whether subtle (infantilization) or overt (neglect, abuse).

Scenario 2. A third-year student on obstetrics and gynaecology is asked by the senior resident to perform an educational pelvic examination on a 41-year-old woman under general anaesthesia for hysterectomy; explicit consent had not been obtained. The resident dismisses the hesitation ("it's something we all have to do", she "doesn't mind"), and a fourth-year clerk obliges. The module's data: in a 2003 survey of 400 Philadelphia medical students, 90% had performed a pelvic exam on an anaesthetized woman; at the University of Oklahoma most students had, but only about a quarter of patients had consented. The questions ask whether prevalence changes the ethics (it does not), whose responsibility consent is, whether the patient must be told, and how hierarchy sustains the practice.

Actionable steps

Dehumanization is unconscious and rooted in old stereotypes, so there is no single fix. Haque and Waytz offer six strategies:

StrategyConstruct
Make patients more identifiable and increase personal responsibilityIndividuation
Give patients a more active role in decision-makingAgency reorientation
Promote common identity to de-emphasize boundariesPromoting similarity
Highlight characteristics that humanize and distinguish patientsPersonification and humanizing procedure
Increase empathyEmpathetic balance and physician selection
Increase moral concern; personify and individualizeMoral engagement

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Well-meaning, not monstrous. The module's thesis is that the therapeutic imperative plus a dehumanized premise produces atrocity.
  • Sterilization then euthanasia then genocide; disabled and mentally ill people first; physicians led.
  • 20 of 23 defendants at the Doctors' Trial were physicians; ten Nuremberg conditions; Helsinki descends from Nuremberg; Belmont (1979) descends from Tuskegee.
  • 1932 to 1972, 600 men, penicillin by 1947: withheld treatment, withheld information, blocked access.
  • 70% TB mortality at some residential schools; 2,800 sterilized under Alberta's Act; 25% versus 2.5% in 1969 to 1972.
  • Prevalence is not consent: 90% of students had done it; a quarter of patients had agreed.
  • Intergenerational trauma was first described in Holocaust survivors' descendants and manifests as complex PTSD.
"Just following orders" and "it's what we all do" are the same defence. Hierarchy plus a mission is the risk structure the module identifies in medicine itself, and the stated obligation is to resist even at personal cost. Silence counts as participation, as the residential-school physicians showed.
Physicians did not abandon medicine to take part in the Holocaust; they redirected it. The protections that followed, the Nuremberg Code and Helsinki, and their North American parallels after Tuskegee, exist because well-meaning doctors dehumanized their patients by degrees, and the same process runs through Canadian residential schools, forced sterilization, and everyday clinical language today.

Across SLM01–07 · WFQ

Integrated Review: Anxiety & Related Disorders, and the Weekly Formative Quiz

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The seven disorders side by side, the drug and therapy maps, the numbers ladder, the pairwise discriminators, the mood and lithium rules the quiz reaches for, and all fifteen quiz items walked through.

The week on one page

Seven disorders share one architecture: a core fear or intrusion, a duration threshold, an avoidance or neutralizing behaviour, and a treatment built on exposure. The differences are what the exam tests.

DisorderCoreThresholdBehaviourFirst-line psychotherapyFirst-line drugs
Specific phobiaA specific object or situationAll of A–G; ≥6 monthsAvoidance or endurance with intense fearCBT with systematic desensitization (graded exposure + relaxation)None: little evidence for medication
Social anxiety disorderNegative evaluation by othersAll of A–J; ≥6 monthsAvoidance of social or performance situationsCBT: cognitive restructuring + exposuresSSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine), venlafaxine XR, pregabalin; performance only: propranolol PRN
Generalized anxiety disorderUncontrollable worry about a number of events≥3 of 6 associated symptoms; more days than not for ≥6 monthsWorry, tension, avoidance of triggersCBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy; therapy equals medicationSSRIs (escitalopram, paroxetine, sertraline), SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine), pregabalin
OCDObsessions and/or compulsions>1 hour/day, marked distress, interferenceCompulsions, including mental actsCBT with exposure and response prevention; equal or superior to drugsSSRIs (escitalopram, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine); second line clomipramine, venlafaxine XR
PTSDExposure to death, serious injury or sexual violenceIntrusion ≥1 of 5, avoidance ≥1 of 2, cognition/mood ≥2 of 7, arousal ≥2 of 6; >1 monthAvoidance of internal and external remindersTrauma-focused CBT; EMDR when TF-CBT is not an optionSSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline), venlafaxine XR
Acute stress disorderSame picture as PTSDWithin the first 30 days; most recoverAs PTSDTime is the only axis the module names between the two
AgoraphobiaFear that escape is difficult or help unavailable≥2 of 5 situations: public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, lines or crowds, being out aloneAvoidance or need for a companionTested on the quiz; not a module this week
Six months is the duration for specific phobia, social anxiety disorder and GAD. One month separates PTSD from acute stress disorder. One hour a day is OCD's criterion B. Only GAD carries a symptom count among the three anxiety disorders; PTSD carries four.

The drug map

Every first-line drug this week is an antidepressant or pregabalin. What changes is which names appear on which list.

DrugSpecific phobiaSocial anxietyGADOCDPTSD

Sertraline—First lineFirst lineFirst lineFirst line

Pregabalin—First lineFirst line——
Propranolol PRN—Performance only———
Clomipramine———Second line—
  • Duloxetine is GAD only. Fluvoxamine is social anxiety and OCD, never GAD. Pregabalin is social anxiety and GAD.
  • Venlafaxine XR is first line in social anxiety, GAD and PTSD but second line in OCD, behind five SSRIs.
  • Sertraline and paroxetine are the two SSRIs on every list except specific phobia.
  • Benzodiazepines are on no first-line list. They are the trap option in GAD ("most evidence": antidepressant) and PTSD (keyed wrong against antidepressant), and they are not first-line maintenance treatment because of tolerance, dependence, cognitive effects and falls.
  • SSRI side effects per the GAD module: GI symptoms, headaches, weight gain and sexual dysfunction. Sexual dysfunction is the keyed common side effect of sertraline on the quiz; tics and dystonia belong to antipsychotics, arrhythmia to tricyclics.
  • OCD dosing doctrine: start low, aim high; response at 6–12 weeks; adequate trial 12–15 weeks; continue at least a year; taper very slowly; the goal is improvement, not remission; relapse is high without behavioural strategies.

The therapy map and the two curves

DisorderTherapyWhat it does
Specific phobiaSystematic desensitizationRank fears 1–10, start at 1/10, graded exposure paired with relaxation, advance once desensitized
Social anxietyCBTCognitive restructuring of maladaptive thoughts plus exposures
GADCBT and MBCTPsychoeducation to prevent avoidance; exposure (extinction), relaxation, biofeedback, imagery also listed
OCDExposure and response prevention12–15 weekly sessions; hierarchy 0–100, start at the bottom, prevent rituals and avoidance
PTSDTrauma-focused CBT; EMDR; cognitive processing therapy; prolonged exposure; stress inoculationDBT is on the list only for self-harm in borderline personality disorder
Panic disorder (quiz)Interoceptive exposureInducing panic in a controlled setting with box-breathing; anxiety falls across exposures by habituation

The mechanism under all of it is the same pair of curves. Performing a compulsion or escaping gives an abrupt drop in anxiety straight back to baseline with the peak unchanged next time: negative reinforcement, and the disorder is maintained. Exposure with response prevention gives progressively lower peaks that resolve sooner, settling onto one low plateau: habituation, because the feared consequence does not occur and anxiety is learned to be time-limited. Avoidance is the behaviour common to every anxiety disorder, which is why exposure is the treatment everywhere. The CBT model is the thoughts, feelings, behaviours triangle with bidirectional arrows; the quiz calls this the cognitive triad, and any option containing "defenses" is psychodynamic and wrong.

Cognitive distortions

DistortionSignature move
Discounting the positiveExplaining away disconfirming positive evidence: "he only invited me to be nice"
CatastrophizationPredicting the worst outcome
OvergeneralizationOne event becomes an always or never rule
LabelingA global negative label on self or others

The numbers ladder

DisorderPrevalenceOnsetSexOther
Specific phobiaMost common mental disorder in women; second in men behind substance-relatedNot givenRanking differs by sexComorbid anxiety, mood, substance disorders
Social anxietySecond most common anxiety disorderMedian 13; 75% between 7 and 15More femalesMost common comorbidity MDD or other anxiety
GAD9% lifetimeMedian 30; the latest of the anxiety disorders2:1 femaleMDD comorbid up to 50%; European descent and developed countries
OCD2–3% lifetimeMean 19.5, earlier peak in males—~10% in first-degree relatives; WHO 10th leading cause of disability; chronic
PTSD9% (quiz band 6–9%)Mid-to-late 20s (band 25–30)2× femaleSuicide risk ×2–3; sexual and relationship violence the commonest source; higher in Aboriginal peoples, refugees, African-Americans

Two traps: 9% belongs to both GAD and PTSD, and 1–3% is OCD's number, planted as a distractor on the PTSD prevalence item. Social anxiety starts in early adolescence, OCD at the end of it, PTSD in the twenties, GAD at thirty.

Pairwise discriminators

  • Specific phobia vs social anxiety: is the feared thing the object or situation itself, or being judged?
  • Specific phobia vs panic disorder: cued and immediate on exposure, or recurrent and unexpected?
  • Agoraphobia vs the others: public transport, open or enclosed spaces, crowds, being out alone, feared because escape is hard. Public speaking is social anxiety; heights and flying are specific phobia.
  • Social anxiety vs GAD: worry confined to social and performance situations, or spread across many activities and uncontrollable?
  • GAD vs OCD: worry about real-life concerns versus recurrent obsessions or compulsions.
  • GAD vs MDD: anxious mood without recurrent low mood, remembering the 50% comorbidity.
  • GAD vs OCPD: episodic uncontrollable worry versus a pervasive early-adult pattern of orderliness, perfectionism and control.
  • GAD vs mania: "racing thoughts" with worry-driven insomnia, fatigue, no grandiosity and no uncharacteristic behaviour is GAD. Mania has decreased need for sleep with preserved energy, grandiosity and impulsive behaviour.
  • OCD vs hoarding, BDD, trichotillomania: hoarding driven by OCD obsessions is OCD; BDD is limited to appearance; trichotillomania is hair pulling without obsessions.
  • OCD vs OCPD: no intrusions and no response-driven rituals in OCPD; both can be diagnosed together.
  • OCD vs tics: compulsions follow obsessions; tics follow premonitory sensory urges.
  • PTSD vs acute stress disorder: more than one month versus the first 30 days.
  • Any of them vs a medical cause: hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, porphyria, CNS neoplasms, and substances including caffeine (moderate intake is 200–300 mg/day; four cups of coffee is about 540 mg). New panic at 70 is an atypical onset and a red flag.

The mood side the quiz tests

Four of the fifteen quiz items reach into the depression and bipolar material from the pre-week videos and the lectures that follow. The facts as the quiz teaches them:

TopicThe rule
Major depressive disorder≥5 of 9 symptoms in the same two-week period, at least one of which is depressed mood or anhedonia. The other seven (appetite, sleep, psychomotor change, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, concentration, thoughts of death) are criteria but not core.
MDD across the lifespanAdolescents often present with irritability rather than sadness; MDD is common in adults; antidepressants are effective in adolescents; new-onset depression in the elderly may signal an emerging neurocognitive disorder.
Manic vs hypomanic episodeMania: ≥1 week (or any duration if hospitalized) of elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy, plus ≥3 symptoms (≥4 if irritable only), with marked functional impairment. Hypomania: ≥4 days, no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalization. One week of irritability, less sleep, talkativeness, grandiosity and inability to complete assignments is a manic episode. Cyclothymia needs two years; mixed features need depressive symptoms.
LithiumCounsel about fine tremor (coarse tremor means toxicity), polyuria and polydipsia, weight gain, hypothyroidism, GI upset, acne. Dose is titrated to trough serum levels, drawn about 12 hours post-dose: not by weight, not by a loading protocol, and not by hepatic function, because lithium is renally cleared. Monitor levels, renal function, thyroid and calcium. Fatty liver belongs to valproate.
Preventing manic relapseA regular sleep cycle. Sleep loss is both a prodrome and a precipitant of mania; exercise is good general advice but not the best answer for manic recurrence.
Biopsychosocial sortingLow self-esteem is psychological; social isolation and belonging to a marginalized population are social; alcohol misuse sorts as biological. The question tests the domain, not whether the item is a risk factor.

The weekly formative quiz, walked through

The quiz does not test OCD, PTSD, suicide risk assessment or disorders due to another medical condition. Four of the seven self-learning modules are absent from it, and four items reach into mood and bipolar material instead. The quiz is not a blueprint for the Mastery Exercise; the modules are.

Threads that run through the week

  • Suicide risk is not confined to its module: PTSD carries a two- to three-fold suicide risk, Canadian residents report 15% past-year suicidal ideation and medical students 11%, and a history of previous attempts is the most powerful predictor at any age. Asking does not increase risk.
  • Medical mimics appear in three modules: GAD's differential names pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism; the medical-condition module gives the full table and the pheochromocytoma remission case; the social anxiety case carries a past history of hyperthyroidism.
  • Substances appear in every case: lorazepam PRN for the flyer, whisky before presentations, four cups of coffee, and the HIV example's three-way split between virus, antiretroviral and drug use.
  • Comorbidity with depression is stated for social anxiety (most common comorbidity), GAD (up to 50%), OCD and PTSD; burnout sits upstream of depression on the wellness continuum.
  • Dehumanizing language about patients with mental illness, substance use or cognitive disability is the ethics module's everyday example, and it is the same population this week's clinical modules describe.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Which drug is on which list: duloxetine GAD only; fluvoxamine social anxiety and OCD; pregabalin social anxiety and GAD; venlafaxine XR second line only in OCD; propranolol only for performance anxiety; nothing for specific phobia.
  • Which number is whose: 9% GAD and PTSD; 2–3% OCD; median 13 social anxiety; 19.5 OCD; 25–30 PTSD; 30 GAD; 2:1 GAD; 2× PTSD.
  • Which count is whose: 3 of 6 GAD; 1/1/2/2 PTSD; 5 of 9 MDD with one core; 2 of 5 situations agoraphobia; 3 symptoms mania (4 if irritable).
  • Which clock is whose: 6 months anxiety disorders; 1 month PTSD; 30 days acute stress; 1 week mania; 4 days hypomania; 2 years cyclothymia; 2 weeks MDD; 1 hour a day OCD.
  • Which therapy is whose: systematic desensitization, ERP, TF-CBT or EMDR, MBCT, interoceptive exposure; DBT is the distractor.
  • CBT plus medication beats medication alone but not CBT alone in OCD; in GAD the two are equivalent; in specific phobia only CBT has evidence.
The anxiety and related disorders differ in what is feared, how long it must last, what is counted, and which names sit on the first-line drug list. Treatment converges on CBT with exposure, whose mechanism is habituation, and on the SSRIs, with venlafaxine XR, duloxetine, pregabalin, propranolol and clomipramine each occupying a specific slot. The quiz tests those slots, the mood and lithium rules from the pre-week material, and the CBT vocabulary; the Mastery Exercise will also test the four modules the quiz leaves out.

Study Suite
★ Do-not-miss · first-step reflexes
Suicidal thoughts disclosed → four steps in order: plan and intent (passive vs active; which pills, access?) → intensity (frequency, practised or aborted attempts, note or will, chosen time or place) → SAD PERSONS → reasons for living. Asking does not increase risk.
Previous attempt → one of the most powerful predictors at every age. Always ask.
New panic at 70, or panic that remits after a pheochromocytoma is removed → anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: time course, atypical features, plausible mechanism. Hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma are the two named mimics.
Mood change two days after a stroke → depressive disorder due to another medical condition. Hopelessness four weeks after a cancer diagnosis → a reaction to the news; the tumour predated it.
One week of irritable mood, less sleep, grandiosity and unable to function → manic episode, not hypomania. Hypomania is ≥4 days without marked impairment.
'Racing thoughts' with fatigue, no grandiosity, no uncharacteristic behaviour → GAD, not bipolar disorder.
Benzodiazepines are on no first-line list; the answer for GAD and PTSD pharmacotherapy is an antidepressant. Specific phobia gets no drug at all.
PTSD-type symptoms in the first 30 days → acute stress disorder; most recover. Beyond one month → PTSD.

Anxiety disorders side by side SLM01–03

Duration for phobia, SAD, GAD ≥6 months, all three
Only one with a symptom count GAD: ≥3 of 6 (restless, fatigued, concentration, irritable, tension, sleep)
Phobia criteria · SAD criteria All of A–G · all of A–J
Phobia specifiers Animal, natural environment, blood-injection-injury, situational, other
SAD specifier Performance only → propranolol PRN
Most common mental disorder in women Specific phobia (2nd in men, behind substance-related)
2nd most common anxiety disorder Social anxiety disorder
SAD onset Median 13; 75% between 7 and 15
GAD numbers 9% lifetime; median onset 30; female 2:1; MDD comorbid up to 50%
GAD begins Later than the other anxiety disorders
Phobia treatment CBT with systematic desensitization; no drug
Desensitization mechanics Rank 1–10, start at 1/10, exposure + relaxation, advance once desensitized
SAD generalized drugs Escitalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine; venlafaxine XR; pregabalin
GAD drugs Escitalopram, paroxetine, sertraline; venlafaxine, duloxetine; pregabalin
GAD 'most evidence' Antidepressant
GAD top two therapies CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy; therapy = medication
SSRI side effects (module) GI, headache, weight gain, sexual dysfunction
Caffeine ceiling 200–300 mg/day; 4 cups coffee ≈ 540 mg

OCD & the related family SLM04

Criterion A Obsessions, compulsions, or both; compulsions include mental acts
Criterion B >1 hour/day, marked distress, interference
Specifiers Insight good/fair · poor · absent/delusional; tic-related
Numbers 2–3% lifetime; mean onset 19.5; ~10% first-degree relatives; WHO 10th cause of disability
Contamination → Washing, checking
Doubting; aggressive or sexual → Checking, reassurance, mental review
Symmetry → Ordering, arranging, 'just so'
Hoarding driven by OCD obsessions Diagnose OCD, not hoarding disorder
BDD · trichotillomania Limited to appearance · hair pulling without obsessions
OCPD No intrusions, no rituals; can coexist with OCD
Tics vs compulsions Premonitory sensory urge vs obsession
First line CBT with ERP, 12–15 weekly sessions; SSRIs escitalopram, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine
Second line Clomipramine; venlafaxine XR
Dosing doctrine Start low aim high; response 6–12 wk; trial 12–15 wk; ≥1 year; taper slowly; improvement not remission
CBT + med vs Beats med alone, not CBT alone
Two curves Compulsion: abrupt drop, same peak. ERP: lower peaks, sooner, one plateau = habituation

PTSD & acute stress SLM05

Criterion A routes Direct, witnessing, learning it happened to a loved one, repeated occupational exposure
Cluster counts Intrusion ≥1/5 · avoidance ≥1/2 · cognition-mood ≥2/7 · arousal ≥2/6
Duration >1 month; acute stress disorder = first 30 days, most recover
Numbers 9% (band 6–9%); 2× female; onset mid-late 20s; suicide ×2–3
Commonest trauma source Sexual and relationship violence
Higher rates Aboriginal peoples, refugees, African-Americans
Most effective therapy Trauma-focused CBT; EMDR when TF-CBT is not an option
Also listed Cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure, stress inoculation; DBT only for self-harm in BPD
First-line drugs Fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline; venlafaxine XR
Keyed wrong Benzodiazepine, ECT, antipsychotic
1–3% distractor That is OCD's number

Suicide risk SLM06

Canada 2013 >4,000 suicides; 9th cause overall; 2nd at ages 15–24
Highest rates Ages 40–59
Gender paradox Females attempt 3–4× more; males die more
Strongest predictor Previous attempts, all ages
SAD PERSONS Sex M, Age <20 or >45, Depression, Previous attempts, Ethanol, Rational thinking loss, Social supports lacking, Organized plan, No spouse, Sickness
Asking increases risk? False; the barrier is the clinician's discomfort
Passive vs active Wish to be dead vs a specific plan
Plan = Feasibility + access to means; be specific
Protective factors Children, spouse, family, pets, religion, self-esteem, therapeutic alliance
Step 4 question 'What has stopped you from acting on these thoughts?'

Due to another medical condition SLM07

Definition Direct pathophysiological consequence; excludes psychosocial reactions
Only criterion that changes A; B–E identical
Criterion E, any of Distress/impairment; hospitalization to prevent harm; psychotic features
Criterion D Not exclusively during delirium
Three diagnostic factors Time course; atypical features (panic at 70); plausible mechanism
Depressive mimics Stroke, TBI, Parkinson's, Cushing's, HIV
Manic mimics Stroke, TBI, Cushing's, MS, HIV, CNS neoplasm
Anxiety mimics Hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, porphyria, CNS neoplasm
HIV three-way Virus → due to AMC; antiretroviral → medication-induced; drug use → substance-induced
Named culprit drugs Prednisone, antiretrovirals

Burden & wellness PW01–02

Lifetime any mental/substance disorder 1 in 3 Canadians
Lifetime mood or anxiety 1 in 5 (21.3%)
Burnout dimensions Emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, low accomplishment
Burnout vs depression Burnout improves away from work; depression is pervasive
Burnout prevalence 24–54% of trainees and professionals
Medical students 27% depression; 11% suicidal ideation; 15.7% seek treatment
US residents 21–43% depression; +16% in first year
Canadian residents (CMA 2018) 38% burnout; 48% depression screen; 15% suicidal ideation
Before training Entrants healthier than peers; training explains the excess
Mata 2015 · Rotenstein 2016 Residents · students + suicidal ideation
Barriers drain into Stigma

Ethics — lessons from the Holocaust SLM08

Thesis Well-meaning physicians, a 'therapeutic imperative', dehumanization
Fritz Klein 'The Jew is the gangrenous appendix in the body of mankind'
Numbers 11 M murdered; 6 M Jews; 250,000 disabled; 200,000 Roma
German doctors >50% early Nazi party members; support without coercion
Escalation Sterilization → euthanasia of disabled and mentally ill → genocide
Doctors' Trial 1946 20 of 23 defendants physicians → Nuremberg Code (10 conditions) → Helsinki
Tuskegee 1932–72 600 Black men; 'bad blood'; penicillin withheld from 1947 → Belmont Report 1979
Residential schools Up to 70% TB deaths at some schools; nutrition experiments on 6 schools
Alberta sterilization 1928–72 >2,800; Indigenous and Métis >25% of sterilized vs 2.5% of population
Syndrome K Fictional diagnosis, Rome 1943, Ossicini; saved dozens
Pelvic exams under anaesthesia 90% of 400 Philadelphia students had done one; ~25% of patients consented
Intergenerational trauma First recognized in Holocaust survivors' descendants; complex PTSD
Haque & Waytz Individuation, agency reorientation, similarity, personification, empathy, moral engagement
